speechtext: Can the Secretary of State for External Affairs answer the question today concerning the functions of the United Nations emergency force in the Gaza strip?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secrefary of Siate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED WITHDRAWAL OF UNEF TO DEMARCATION LINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to my hon. friend's question I should like to make the following statement. The legal rights of Egypt in the administration of the Gaza strip derive from the armistice agreement between Egypt and Israel signed in 1949 and confirmed by the United Nations. If these legal rights are ignored or rejected, then the armistice agreement is violated. But the United Nations assembly has affirmed by more than one resolution, including that of February 2 which was carried unanimously, that the armistice provisions, all of them, should be scrupulously observed.
The responsibilities and functions of the United Nations in the Gaza strip come from assembly resolutions and are reinforced by the practical necessities of the situation. These responsibilities and functions in our opinion should be accepted by Egypt, which should fully co-operate with the United Nations in their discharge. If Egypt is unwilling to co-operate in this way, then the United Nations' task in Gaza becomes impossible and the matter in our opinion should be referred at once to the United Nations assembly.
Our position, Mr. Speaker, which has been stated more than once in New York and in this house, is that the United Nations should be associated to the maximum possible extent in the administration of the Gaza strip. I regret that this was not made clear and definite in a resolution of the United Nations assembly which would have specified the arrangements to follow the withdrawal of

Inquiries of the Ministry Israeli forces. Why that was not done, Mr. Speaker, I attempted to explain a week ago today. It should be recalled also that the United Nations already accepts full responsibility for more than 200,000 Arab refugees in Gaza.
The problem then, as I see it, is to find an acceptable balance in the administration of Gaza between the practical position which the United Nations must take and the legal position of Egypt under the armistice agreement. Any such "suitable balance" in particular must give the United Nations that control of internal security in the Gaza strip necessary to enable it to carry out effectively its operations and responsibilities on the demarcation line. So far as the Canadian government is concerned, UNEF could not be expected to discharge effectively its duty of preventing raids and incursions and maintain peaceful conditions along that line if it were not in a position to carry out observations or investigations and to exercise necessary control in the strip itself. A satisfactory agreement to this effect is a fundamental prerequisite of the effective continuance of UNEF's role on the demarcation line. If no such agreement is made and kept, there will not only be renewed trouble between Israel and Egypt but the continued operation of UNEF will be prejudiced. Certainly it would be difficult for Canada to continue to participate in the force under conditions-and we hope those conditions will not materialize -in which it would not be able to discharge satisfactorily the responsibilities given to it by the United Nations assembly. We have made this position clear more than once to the secretary general and to the advisory committee in New York as recently as last week.
The secretary general is at the moment engaged in very important discussions with the governments immediately concerned. As yet we have had only a preliminary report concerning the discussions which are now going on in Cairo, but that report has been enough to cause us to question the accuracy of certain Cairo press messages about these talks.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure the house hopes, that these discussions will clear up the difficulties that face the United Nations in this area. Otherwise the results will be serious for United Nations' action there and perhaps even for peace between the conflicting states. At the conclusion of his talk the secretary general will report to the committee of seven, of which Canada is a member, which will no doubt then consider in the light of that report whether a meeting of the full assembly is required.

speakerposition: stagedirection

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Is he now in a position to answer a question I asked about pressures exerted by the Chinese communist government on Chinese abroad?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON CAMPAIGN FOR REMITTANCES OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE BY NATIONALS ABROAD
speechtext:
Yes. The hon. member
asked this question some weeks ago-and it required a good deal of investigation- whether my department had taken note of reported intensified efforts on the part of the communist authorities in Peking to compel or exert influence upon Chinese abroad to send remittances to communist China and also what action the Canadian government proposes to take in the light of that reported intensified campaign.
As I said last February, Mr. Speaker, we have seen the press and other reports bearing on this subject. Last June there was a conference on overseas Chinese affairs in Peking, attended by representatives of overseas Chinese, their dependents living in China, and an organization created by the communist Peking authorities called the commission for overseas Chinese affairs. An official of the latter organization at that meeting in Peking made certain criticisms of the way in which dependents of overseas Chinese and overseas Chinese who had returned to their native provinces to retire had been treated by the communist party workers and officials.
Subsequent to this the Chinese government announced its intention of removing the abuses on which this criticism was based. I cannot form any opinion as to the degree to which they have succeeded in this professed intention. However, as the intention of the Peking authorities appears to have been to create a favourable climate for remittances rather than to threaten dire consequences to relations in China if remittances are not forthcoming, it may be that the lot of the dependents of overseas Chinese has improved to some degree, although not likely to the degree the Peking authorities profess to wish.
The hon. member asked what action the Canadian government proposes to take in the light of the alleged intensified campaign. The only action the Canadian government

could take-and I am not sure that it would be desired either by Canadian citizens with dependents in China or by the public at large-would be to institute a system of foreign exchange control. It would probably not serve a useful purpose to initiate exchange restrictions relating to communist China alone, because such restrictions could be evaded comparatively easily though at increased cost to those desiring to send remittances.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON CAMPAIGN FOR REMITTANCES OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE BY NATIONALS ABROAD

speechtext: Yes, we will, Mr. Speaker, and we shall secure all the information we can although in this we are under some handicap because of course we have no representation in communist China.

speechtext:
On March 20 the Leader of the Social Credit party asked the following question:
How did employees of the Department of National Revenue become involved in supplying information to certain United States citizens concerning
Inquiries of the Ministry Premium Iron Ores Limited and its accounts and income tax returns? Who gave them authority to supply this information?
I wish to make the following detailed answer. The commissioner of internal revenue of the United States of America made application to the Canadian taxation authorities to furnish information required by his officers to complete investigations being conducted of Premium Iron Ores Limited and certain United States citizens, and in so doing invoked the provisions of article XIX of the Canada-United States tax convention. This article reads as follows:
With a view to the prevention of fiscal evasion, each of the contracting states undertakes to furnish to the other contracting state, as provided in the succeeding articles of this convention, the information which its competent authorities have at their disposal or are in a position to obtain under its revenue laws in so far as such information may be of use to the authorities of the other contracting state in the assessment of the taxes to which this convention relates.
The information to be furnished under the first paragraph of this article, whether in the ordinary course or on request, may be exchanged directly between the competent authorities of the two contracting states.
The officers of my department furnished the information requested as they were required to do under the terms of the article as quoted above.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening before adjournment I was referring to a statement made by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) in his address on the budget. In his speech he quoted a statement made by the labour chancellor of the exchequer, Philip Snowden, apparently with approval,


to the effect that any government that takes half a crown more than it needs is guilty of getting money under false pretences. First I want to suggest that apparently the hon. member for Greenwood has failed to appreciate the various functions that a modern budget can perform and that these functions are not confined solely to the collection of revenues and the estimation of expenditures.
A modern budget is an instrument that can be used to control the level of income and employment and can be used effectively to control inflation or deflation. For that reason, and viewed in that light, a budget which announces a surplus cannot be taken as a sign of improvidence or imprudence. As a matter of fact, in the light of present conditions in Canada and in the light of modern fiscal policy the surplus at present declared in these circumstances can be regarded as a prudent and wise declaration of policy by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris).
However, Mr. Speaker, my main remarks this morning will be directed to an appreciation of those parts of the budget having to do with the maritime provinces. I believe that the proposals in the budget are proposals of great dimensions and will have far-reaching effects on the economies of the maritime provinces. I am disappointed that spokesmen for the official opposition have chosen to belittle these proposals and seem to have failed to understand the historical background and the current problems that have given rise to these specific proposals in the budget.
I made reference last night to the fact that the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), addressing a political meeting in my riding the day before yesterday and as reported in a Halifax newspaper, had stated that the proposals for the maritimes in the present budget were in reality things that the Conservative party had been advocating all along and that the only complaint that he had was that the timing was wrong or that the introduction of these proposals had been delayed. This view of the budget taken by the leader of the official opposition was undoubtedly influenced by the atmosphere of receptivity which he found in the province of Nova Scotia and which would likely induce the hon. member for Greenwood, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and, indeed, the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell), to change their appreciation of the budget if they also journeyed to the province of Nova Scotia.
These proposals are not nebulous proposals in any sense of the term. These proposals do not lack detail, as suggested by the hon. member for Greenwood. These proposals are not a carrot, as suggested by the hon.

member for Greenwood. They reveal a great deal, and not very little as suggested by the hon. member for Greenwood. I believe that a consideration of the two proposals having to do with transportation and power development will bear out the contention that the budget will have very fundamental repercussions on the economy of Nova Scotia.
The government of Canada, Mr. Speaker, has always been conscious of the need to provide a proper transportation policy in relation to the province of Nova Scotia. In his budget speech the Minister of Finance referred to the fact that the government is now making substantial payments on the movement of maritime and Nova Scotia coal to the central markets of Canada. Furthermore, the central government has been making helpful payments for the movement of feed grain into the province of Nova Scotia, and if you consult the estimates for this year you will find that the government has estimated an expenditure of roughly $13 million for the movement of goods under the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
In the past year the assistance given to the coal industry under the subvention policy reaches an amount of $8 million while the total paid for the movement of Nova Scotia coal since the inception of this policy is in the neighbourhood of $64 million. These figures I have quoted are correct and reflect the fact that the central government has been keenly interested in the transportation problem of the maritime provinces.
In the budget address the Minister of Finance suggests that an immediate review of maritime transportation problems will be undertaken. He suggests further that action will be taken to increase payments under the Maritime Freight Rates Act by 10 per cent restoring the comparable level of assistance as it existed in the immediate postwar period. I believe that in order to understand the significance of this proposal one should examine for a moment the historical background of the introduction of the Maritime Freight Rates Act in 1927.
As all hon. members know, one of the terms of union in 1867 was a promise written into the British North America Act that an intercolonial railway would be built to link the eastern provinces with central Canada, and this intercolonial railway was regarded as absolutely necessary in order to implement the dream of the fathers of confederation that a national market should be created in the new country. As hon. members are aware, construction of the intercolonial railway was determined by strategic and imperial considerations which added well over 200 82715-165
22, 1957
The Budget-Mr. MacEachen miles to a route that would ordinarily be built, barring these considerations.
With the passage of time it was apparent in the maritime provinces and in Nova Scotia that the intercolonial railway was not indeed carrying out the expectations held for it at the time of confederation. As hon. members will recall, before 1927 Sir Andrew Rae Duncan presided over a royal commission on maritime claims and it was from his just and fertile mind that recommendations were made in the transportation field that were embodied in 1927 in the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
Since that time the level of assistance has been held at 20 per cent and it is now to be raised to 30 per cent pending a complete investigation into the transportation problem of the maritime provinces. I should like to refer particularly to one sentence in the paragraph dealing with transportation where the Minister of Finance suggests that as a result of a study of transportation it might be possible for the Atlantic region to get more value from the present level of federal expenditures in this field and from any of the increased funds that might become available.
It is apparent that the assistance given to the coal industry and under the Maritime Freight Rates Act are based upon historical considerations and it should be one of the first tasks of any inquiry to establish whether the present level of assistance available to the maritime provinces could be employed more usefully on the basis of modern and present day economic developments in the maritime provinces. The suggestion has been made that this inquiry should devote itself to a consideration of a special assistance for special products. For example, the Crows-nest pass rates assist the grain growers of Canada in a special way and I have in mind that if similar assistance could be made available to the steel industry of Nova Scotia in that way it would assert a special comparative advantage for that industry in competition with the steel plants of central Canada.
There is nothing nebulous about this proposal; there is nothing lacking in detail because the proposal made by the minister is in line with the consistent attitude of the government to retain and maintain the particular conditions conferred upon the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick under the terms of union of 1867.
I want to say a word about the proposal in the budget for the development of thermal power plants in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. In the winter of 1954 the dominion coal board, which had been studying constantly the problem of thermal power in

The Budget-Mr. MacEachen the maritime provinces, asked Professor Christie, an outstanding thermal power expert at Johns Hopkins University in the United States, to study the problems of power development in the Atlantic provinces in its relation to the coal industry. In September 1954 Professor Christie submitted his report to the dominion coal board and it is upon the full details of that report that the suggestion in the budget is based. I suggest that those in the official opposition who find these proposals nebulous and lacking in detail should study that report which is the basis of the recommendations in the budget.
I think it is clear that future power development in Nova Scotia depends upon the use of coal and thermal development. It is clear also that in New Brunswick there are future possibilities in the field of hydro development. As Professor Christie suggests, these two provinces are complementary as regards power resources and for that reason it was suggested that greater economy and efficiency could be reached by an interconnection of the power systems of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. On pages 9 and 10 of his report Professor Christie gives at least ten reasons why this interconnection and consolidation should occur.
Not only has the federal government endorsed this proposal, it has stated in the budget that these thermal power plants will be built, provided the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick agree to the proposal. Three years ago this proposal was made by Professor Christie who in the concluding paragraph of his report said that in order to realize this advantage for the maritime provinces real statesmanship will be required. I quote from his report: Real statesmanship will be necessary to realize such a consolidation as local politics and provincial pride will oppose such a move.
The real statesmanship called for by Professor Christie was provided by the Minister of Finance in this far-reaching proposal. It is now up to the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to participate in this imaginative and forward-looking proposal which in my view is fraught with the same consequences for Nova Scotia as the gas pipeline holds for other parts of Canada.
First of all, cheap power is an important factor in industrial development. While efforts have been made to provide power in our provinces we know that cheaper power could be a compensating attraction to industry which might wish to locate in that area. We know also that from the first effect of this proposal there will follow a second effect, the stimulus to the coal industry in Nova Scotia.

In his report Professor Christie suggested that in ten years the consumption of coal for thermal development would increase by half a million tons per year. If you examine the proposals in the budget for the maritime provinces you will find that they form what I would regard as a correlated attack on the problem of the development of our provinces. First of all, they attempt to overcome the transport factor which in the minds of most economists is the most important single factor in industrial location. Then these proposals tackle the problem of power in the only constructive manner in which it can be tackled, given the resources and the fuel supplies in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Combined with that there is the obvious stimulus given to the coal industry which now requires greater markets and greater assistance.
I certainly do not share the views which have been expressed by members of the official opposition that this budget is a disappointment for the maritime provinces. I believe that this budget is constructive and if there is any disappointment to any group in the house it can come only from a knowledge that this budget has been received very warmly by the people of the province of Nova Scotia, with whose views I keep in touch.
Mr. Speaker, I want, for a moment, to speak about one or two matters that fall into the same category but of a less general application. I have always felt that economic development could proceed through the enunciation of general policies and also through the establishment of particular projects that might have a local application, and that might assist in stimulating economic development in certain areas. I want to refer to an item in the supplementary estimates which appeared under the Department of Public Works. The funds available from this item will have very important repercussions to an important part of the county of Inverness. I refer to the decision taken by the Department of Public Works to go ahead with the erection of a breakwater causeway between the mainland of Port Hood and the island of Port Hood.
There is interesting history involved in this project. At one time there was a natural land bridge joining these two land areas, but with the passage of time this bridge was removed through erosion and wave action. A splendid harbour which had supported a large fishing fleet was completely or almost completely destroyed. The residents of the area have been working since 1906 to have the federal government undertake the restoration of this harbour by the erection of a breakwater causeway. I am happy to say that their dream extending back to 1906 has been realized

through the fine co-operation given to this project by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters). Last week when I visited this area I was told on all sides that the decision to go ahead with this project will mean a great stimulus to the southern part of Inverness county. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that in this case, although not as important in itself as the problem of power development, there lies a model that we could usefully follow in trying to rebuild certain parts of the economy of Nova Scotia.
For a moment, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer to a proposal put forward to the government in Nova Scotia and the federal government by the farmers of eastern Nova Scotia. Recently eastern co-operative services and Cape Breton co-operative services amalgamated their business into a single administration. They undertook the amalgamation in order to provide increased marketing facilities for the farmers of eastern Nova Scotia. At present there are large quantities of agricultural products imported into eastern Nova Scotia while agriculture in that area is not in the position in which we would like to see it. In order to overcome this difficulty, there is a proposal to build a processing plant in eastern Nova Scotia to provide a market outlet for those farmers. This requires assistance from the government in order to have it established. It is a place where there could be fruitful federal and provincial co-operation. Marketing is primarily a provincial responsibility, and for that reason it is up to the provincial government at this stage to announce its assistance for this project in order to put members of parliament from eastern Nova Scotia in a proper constitutional position to press a claim for assistance against the federal treasury in Ottawa. I do believe that if this action is taken initially by the provincial government it will assist in Ottawa in putting forward the claim of assistance from these producers.
I intended, Mr. Speaker, to say something about the social benefits, and in particular about the amendment proposed by the C.C.F. group. However, I fear that my time is drawing to a close. I shall simply refer for a moment to this amendment and to the suggestion by the C.C.F. group that the old age pension should be increased to an amount commensurate with the increase in the gross national product since 1949, which would call for a pension of approximately $75 per month.
I do not intend to comment upon the validity of associating pension raises with the gross national product or with any other economic quantity that could be employed. But I would like to suggest that if further action is desired, there is another source 82715-1651
The Budget-Mr. MacEachen from which this action can be had. I understand that when the constitution was amended in order to provide for old age security, the provinces of Canada reserved to themselves their capacity to take action in this field in the future and protected the action they had already taken. In that way the provinces have recognized their jurisdiction and, automatically, their responsibility. The federal government has responded to the requests made upon it to increase social benefits. The provincial governments also have recognized responsibilities in this field. I would suggest with all earnestness that the advocates of greater pensions from the C.C.F. group might use their influence with the province of Saskatchewan to come forward now with greater supplemental benefits. I would suggest to those people in the official opposition who have influence with the premiers of Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia that they have those provinces come forward with increased supplemental benefits.
I have made some investigations into the system in Saskatchewan. While I certainly would not attempt to say I have the intimate knowledge of that province possessed by the members from that province, I find that the supplemental system in Saskatchewan is somewhat puzzling. I understand, for example, that no assistance is available to the recipients of old age assistance; in other words, those in the category from 65 to 69 receive no supplemental assistance from the provincial treasury of that province. It would seem that if there is a desire to assist any needy group, Saskatchewan and its friends here might do something along that line. I am aware that the supplemental assistance available to persons over 70, or old age security, extends from $2.50 to $20 for those in the most favoured assistance range.
There are roughly 47,000 receiving old age security in the province of Saskatchewan and of these roughly 17,000 receive supplemental benefits, while 4,925 who receive old age assistance receive no supplemental benefits at all. Therefore, while this amendment is interesting and certainly appealing, I suggest that this problem of greater assistance for the aged is one that is as intimately connected with provincial responsibilities as it is with federal responsibilities, and that the account taken in this budget, which is evident in its wholesome effects, can be followed up in the provincial legislatures which have reserved their own prerogatives in this field of supplemental assistance. I make this suggestion, not in any effort to annoy my friends from Saskatchewan, but in an effort to clarify a problem which sometimes seems to get rather confused.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a loyal Scot and one whose ancestors came from the Highlands, and not too far removed, I could not help but be very interested in the closing remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration said the other day in the house that these people were showing excellent judgment in the idea that they come to Newfoundland. I could not help but think that if they come to Newfoundland the people of Newfoundland will be very lucky indeed. His remarks about the Gaelic language reminded me of an incident in my undergraduate days in university. There was a certain teacher there with whom I never seemed to get along very well; I never seemed to be able to get through to him. Finally, one day I was leaving his office to go home for Christmas holidays and he said good-bye to me in Gaelic. I am not going to use the term here because Hansard could not spell it and I am not sure that I could help them to spell it correctly, but I replied in kind. He said, "Come back here, young fellow; where did you learn to speak Gaelic?" I will drop the story there, but the ensuing conversation very quickly and very effectively fixed up any breach that there ever was between my professor and myself.
In my opening remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say something about a matter that I think should be of interest to all hon. members. For some years now the Prince Edward Island historical society has been advocating that space be set aside in our capital city of Charlottetown for a provincial museum. To date that desire has not been realized. Recently, the president of that society and the council of Charlottetown

board of trade asked me to look into the possibilities of a development that would be in keeping with the desire for a provincial museum and in keeping with the thoughts of Canadians who rightfully wish to preserve buildings and sites which have played an important part in our national development.
The suggestion is that the provincial building in Charlottetown should be taken over by the historic sites and monuments board and made a national shrine. It includes also the suggestion that somewhere in that building a space should be set aside for this museum.
For the benefit of hon. members who are not familiar with our provincial building, I might explain that this is the building where the first conference on confederation was held. In a room on the second floor which we refer to as confederation chamber a meeting was held on September 1, 1864 of representatives from the maritime provinces and from Canada, as the term was loosely applied to the general area which comprises Ontario and Quebec today. There in that room in our provincial building this great country of Canada was conceived and there was laid the foundation for our confederation.
Now it is true perhaps that the actual birth of confederation took place at Quebec a little later for there the actual pact of confederation was signed. I suggest that the need of preserving our building in Charlottetown is highlighted and emphasized by the fact that the building which housed that meeting in Quebec no longer stands. It has been lost to the nation and to posterity so that our building at home is now the only real link with confederation that remains.
I have discussed the idea with leading public men in several of our provinces and on each and every occasion they have agreed it would be a splendid idea.

speechtext:
"It would be a crime to lose that historic building; it should be preserved through the years," one man told me recently here in Ottawa.
If I may digress for a moment, I might say that the latter statement was made to me in Ottawa recently just after I had listened to our St. Dunstan's debating team win the national intercollegiate title. I am very proud of that feat. The coach of the team Rev. Fred Cass, happens to be an old football pal of mine which perhaps gives me a greater personal interest in it. I am also proud to say
The Budget-Mr. Matheson that this is the second national title they have captured in five years. Indeed since 1950 they have been national finalists once and reached the semi-finals on one other occasion in addition to winning two titles. Getting back to my subject, I might say that the proper approach with respect to the preservation of this building is through the historic sites and monuments board. I have made that approach through the Prince Edward Island representative, Hon. Chief Justice Thane A. Campbell.
However, as the development eventually would come under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the department to which the historic sites and monuments board is responsible, I thought it fitting to take this opportunity of putting this reference to the proposal on the pages of our country's parliamentary record.
I have discussed the proposal with our premier at home and he has expressed agreement in principle. There are, of course, certain reservations. He would, for example, want to retain the legislative assembly in this historic building. I feel that most of us would agree that this should be done.
I do not think there is anything further I should add at this time. I am sure that most hon. members will agree that the proposal is sound, and that it is in keeping with our wish to retain and cherish places and memories that are closely linked with our historic past.
The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) made a statement in the house during the course of this session which may have reflected on the quality of the bacon hogs we produce in Prince Edward Island. Let me say right away that I know he did not intend it that way and I do not charge him with that intent but I think I should say a word or two about our bacon hog quality.
The figures for last year which are the most recent figures I have indicate that our province again topped all other Canadian provinces in the percentage of top grade hogs. Our provincial swine breeders have been doing that consistently for some years now and last year they set a new all-time record for the excellence of their bacon products; 57.9 per cent of all Prince Edward Island hogs shipped through inspection plants were graded A or top quality. This corresponds with 54.1 per cent in 1955, 51.4 per cent in 1953 and 35 per cent in 1941.
There has been a general improvement in bacon hog quality right across the country although other provinces do not closely approach our breeders in top quality. If I may cite the figures for last year only they indicate that Nova Scotia breeders were closest

The Budget-Mr. Matheson to ours with 52.5 per cent in top grade, New Brunswick was next with 49.9 per cent, Ontario was a rather weak fourth with 35 per cent and the others trailed well behind with Alberta's 21.3 per cent at the bottom of the scale. The all-Canadian average was 30 per cent, but even this is an improvement over the all-Canadian average of 28.5 in 1955 and the same percentage in 1953.
I might point out that these figures were taken from the official report prepared by H. W. Clay, senior livestock fieldman for the federal Department of Agriculture at Charlottetown. Mr. Clay is a man who grew up with the developing swine industry at home and one who, at the official level, is very closely concerned with it and shares in the credit for its great progress.
A neighbour of mine, L. W. Roper, has been a strong and a consistently effective livestock fieldman through the years, and he has made a great contribution. Since I have mentioned these two gentlemen I should not overlook mentioning the other member of the staff, Jim Mundy, who comes from Alberta. The popularity of this likeable young fieldman indicates to us at home that something really good can still come out of the west.
I want to thank the member from Wellington South (Mr. Hosking) for the very fine tribute he paid to our island bacon hogs here last year. He noted that although they did not place in the live classes at the royal winter fair when they showed there several years ago, they did score very heavily in the dressed carcass competition at the same fair. He noted-and I agree with him-that there is something wrong with the system of judging when animals that top all other competition in the carcass classes are so completely overlooked by the judges in the live classes.
The royal winter fair is our top agricultural fair. It has been properly named the show window of Canadian agriculture, yet there is evidently some marked improvement needed in its method of judging when such a thing can and does happen.
I know personally of several royal shows there where our hogs were not placed on the hoof in breeding classes and yet island hogs cleaned up in both the Brethour and Todd trophy competition for dressed bacon. It is so evident that there is an inexcusable inconsistency there that I am not going to say anything more about it.
Before I leave the subject, I should note that the member from Saskatoon had observed that he had seen very low grade western grain being ground for feed for our island hogs. The feed came from our grain


growing prairie provinces. Anything he or other hon. members from that area can do to help our farmers get a better grade of feed grain would be appreciated.
The hon. member himself told me privately that it was the fault of some of our feed mixers in the east, because they buy a low grade of grain. If that is so, they have no reason to be proud of their action or their product.
Prior to the two freight rate increases of seven and four per cent respectively the freight on a ton of feed from the head of the lakes to Charlottetown was $17.80. Of that amount the federal government, through the feed grain freight assistance policy, paid $12.80. The farmer paid $5.
After the two freight rate increases went into effect, the freight from the head of the lakes to the maritimes was $19.80 and the farmer had to pay $7. Now the situation is that the federal government pays $14.25 per ton leaving $5.50 to be paid by the farmer. On top of that now, of course, we have the 50 per cent increase in the assistance under the Maritime Freight Rates Act on traffic originating in the maritimes and outward bound.
These two developments, Mr. Speaker, will do a great deal to bring a much needed measure of relief to our producers. It will help all our people including our manufacturers, but I am thinking more particularly now of our primary producers, and especially those in my own province who grow and ship heavy, bulky products on which the freight is a very large item indeed. It will be valuable, for example, to our potato producers who have had some difficult times during the past years.
I note that Howard Mann, executive manager of the maritime transportation commission, viewed the increased freight assistance with delight, to use his term. He said it was "the first real break in our freight wall in 30 years."
I note with approval too that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) observed in his speech that "a change of this kind will only go part way toward meeting the transportation problems of the Atlantic provinces." There is satisfaction too in his indication that the over-all transportation needs are being studied with a view to further action. We agree that further action is needed and we shall keep pressing for that further action.
There are other problems of agriculture. There are many of them. But my discussions with the people here indicate to me that many of them are receiving serious and sympathetic consideration.
The house is aware of the move to adjust the potato tariff structure more favourably

for our Canadian growers. Like my hon. friend the member for Kings (Mr. Kiekham), who is himself a moderately large potato grower, I have followed this question closely ever since it was introduced some two years ago. I am still keeping in close touch with it, and I am satisfied that the appropriate departmental people here are doing what they can to get a favourable adjustment along the lines of the request made by representatives of the potato industry right across the country.
I am spending considerable time on agriculture, Mr. Speaker, and I do so because it is of major importance to our province. I hear spokesmen from other provinces suggest that difficulties in agriculture affect adversely that particular phase of their provincial economy. But in our case, I will be exaggerating only very slightly if I say that agriculture is the whole of our economy. Certainly, it is our basic economy, and if it is not prospering our people cannot prosper. It is true that we have an important fishing industry in Prince Edward Island, and here I want to refer with appreciation to the unemployment insurance benefits being made available to fishermen.
We also have a growing tourist industry. If the investigations now under way concerning the proposed causeway between our province and New Brunswick indicate that this project is financially feasible, we shall have a much greater tourist industry. But, for the present, agriculture is our main source of revenue. Unless it prospers, our province cannot prosper.
One of the recent handicaps under which agricultural producers are labouring is caused by a lot of ridiculous nonsense being written about diet and about the use of non-fattening foods. Hundreds of self-styled diet experts are trying to reap a profit by writing a lot of senseless junk about dieting principles. Some of them talk about food values without even the slightest knowledge of what they are discussing.
The result is that some people are being induced to stop using some of our most valuable food products. I believe that dairy products are, perhaps, most adversely affected.
Recently there seems to be almost an organized campaign against the use of whole milk. They talk about skim milk, and about fat-free milk, and about a lot of other similar nonsense. Mr. Speaker, I could quote you a number of eminent medical scientists who have made a study of this problem and whose findings indicate that milk still is one of our most valuable and necessary basic foods.
Dr. V. E. Collum, Johns Hopkins University, says for example: "The people who have achieved, who have become large, strong,
The Budget-Mr. Matheson vigourous people, who have reduced the infant mortality, who have the best trades in the world, who are progressive in science and in every activity of human intellect, are people who have used liberal amounts of milk and its products."
I have read numerous books and quotations by people who suggest that one cannot avoid overweight or reduce on a diet which includes whole milk. I can disprove that, Mr. Speaker, from personal experience. I have taken off weight very successfully-indeed fairly rapidly-and drank a quart to a quart and one half of whole milk a day while I was doing it. Rarely a day passes when I do not drink that much milk, and I do not think anyone could suggest I have any overweight problems now.
Let me cite for you a more scientific authority. Dr. John J. Miller is director of nutritional research of Medical Dairy Specialties, Incorporated, Chicago, Illinois. He notes that it is a burning question whether milk fat is going to "win out" in the debate over the causes of heart disease. I am now quoting Dr. Miller:
To understand the critical nature ol the disease, we must take a look at the causes of so-called heart disease. Actually, we are speaking not of a disease but of heart failure. This arises from poor circulation or a complete lack of circulation of blood.
The basic causes of the heart trouble we are discussing include a thickening or hardening of the arteries. Perhaps the most apparent chemical "villain" causing thickening or hardening of the arteries is cholesterol. It is a white, fatty crystalline alcohol which is found in food fats, and which is formed from other fats and nutrients in the body.
It was discovered a few years ago that improper use of fat by the body was a factor in the formation of these cholesterol patches in human arteries. Since then there has been a gradual build-up of misinformation and prejudice, among laymen and professional people alike, as to the role of milk fats as a possible cause of this abnormal condition in the arteries.
I am quoting from Dr. Miller, Mr. Speaker, but because of limited time I can only quote bits and pieces of his article. I am, however, trying to be fair and accurate. If any hon. member wishes to read the entire article I shall be glad to make it available to him.
Turning to the nutritional phases of the problem, he says, in part:
If whole milk and its products, all containing butter fat, are a menace to the health of the nation, then all people should be informed of this fact. On the other hand, if this is not true, and if whole milk is fully nutritious and health-promoting at all ages, then the entire nation should be aroused. The campaign of misinformation about milk and dairy products should be stopped immediately.
Continuing, Dr. Miller says:
The crux of the issue is as follows:

The Budget-Mr. Matheson
And he lists his findings in nine paragraphs. I can only quote a few of them. Here they are:
High human consumption of total fats cannot be correlated directly with thickening or hardening of the arteries.
The type of fat consumed has more to do with injury to blood vessels than the amount of fat involved.
The amount of cholesterol in the blood is not a measure of the amount deposited in the walls of the arteries.
And listen to this one:
Thickening of the arteries is a modern disease, especially of the last 20 years, whereas whole milk has been a healthful, basic dietary food for more than 2,000 years.
The increased incidence of hardening of the arteries and its severity may possibly be correlated with the greatly increased consumption of "hardened" vegetable oils and with the decline in intake of milk and butter.
There is more, Mr. Speaker, but I think 1 have quoted enough to indicate the general nature of Dr. Miller's contention. I might add that he is a man of wide experience who is, apparently, highly regarded by medical scientists. He is at present a member of the committee on nutrition of the Illinois State Medical Society, and he was formerly editor of Chemical Abstracts, a publication international in scope. He is also a member of various scientific organizations and the author of numerous treatises. He has lectured on nutrition before many medical meetings throughout the United States.
Mr. Speaker, I referred a while ago to the fishing industry. With the co-operation of Department of Public Works officials both here and at home we have been building and developing wharves and other harbour installations in an effort to help the fisheries development. Some real progress is being made, but there is still a great deal to be done.
Rustico, the biggest fishing area in my riding, has had a harbour problem for years. A sand bar at the harbour's mouth has barred it to all but shallow draught boats. Developments now under way will, we hope, remove this handicap. When that goal is realized, this harbour will be able to handle draggers and the fishing and processing potential will be greatly increased. Then it will, possibly, be challenging for leadership a place like Souris, in the riding of the hon. member for Kings. The advent of the dragger has caused a major development in that town.
Before I close, Mr. Speaker, I would like to express my appreciation for the increase in veterans pensions, and the increased benefits available under war veterans allowances. We owe our veterans a debt of gratitude that we can never fully repay.

It is something that we must never forget. We must never allow our children to forget it either.
I should like also to thank the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources for the improvements that are being made in our national park in Prince Edward Island. The appointment of a full-time superintendent is a major forward step, and in Fred Browning, the present superintendent, we have a man who is taking a keen interest in the development of the park.
The construction of the gulf shore drive is a major undertaking. It is linking the various parts of our park and will, I suggest, be a major factor in our future tourist development. The road runs along our beautiful north shore and will, when completed, be one of the most beautiful drives that can be found anywhere in the country.
A delegation from the Atlantic provinces economic council met the government in Ottawa this week. The council, generally known as APEC, is relatively new but I have great hopes for it. It has attracted some capable and busy men who are finding time from their own businesses to devote to this general effort towards self-help for that area. In their presentation to the government the council spokesmen indicated that although they have no notion of interfering in dominion-provincial relationships they are prepared to place their full resources at the disposal of the federal and provincial governments in assessing any situation in which joint government action is contemplated. I am sorry that more of our Atlantic members do not give it their vocal support here.
I know it is impossible to include in a budget speech everything that everyone wants, but I think that perhaps the most regretted omission of all is the failure to include any reference to increased allowances for retired civil servants. I am thinking now particularly of the widows of several former civil servants whom I know personally and of the difficulty they are having in making ends meet on the portion of the retirement allowance which was left to them when their husbands passed on. This is one problem which I would earnestly commend to the attention of the minister and his colleagues for the earliest possible future action.

Our criticisms of the government are of three kinds. (1) In some important ways it has paid too little attention to the interests of western Canada ... Liberalism as we see it today! The problem which really faces the country is that of inflation. As found at pages 2215 and 2216 of Hansard of March 14 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) said:

That, Mr. Speaker, is a euphemism for a higher cost of living for consumers all across the country, and apparently there is no legislation whatsoever envisaged by the government whereby inflation can be combatted. Despite the recommendations of the governor

Stewart of the Bank of Canada, despite his statement that inflation cannot be combatted only by monetary means, the government is insisting on taking no fiscal measures to combat a serious menace to the welfare of the Canadian people. The government has tried to combat inflation by means of monetary controls, a hit-or-miss method, a bull in a china shop method, one which is not selective at all, with the result that one segment of our economy has been affected more than any other. I refer, of course, to the building of homes for the people of Canada. This is going to be rectified to some extent.
Despite the fact the minister tells us we are in an inflationary period, the Bank of Canada is going to make available to the chartered banks another $15 million approximately so that their cash reserves can be increased, and the net effect will be an increase of bank credit of anything up to $150 million. Granted that is going to be used for house building, granted that is a legitimate and proper thing; nevertheless it is going to increase the inflationary trend in the country unless the government takes fiscal measures to reduce spending in other segments of the economy.
In the past we have been dependent mostly on our life insurance companies for mortgage money. Then the banks were brought into line in 1954. I remember arguing in the house at that time that the banks would only lend up to a certain sum of money in absolute terms and then they would stop. I said 7 per cent of savings. That, of course, has happened. Apparently the banks came to the conclusion that they were prepared to lend between 7 per cent and 8 per cent of their savings deposits to home builders in this country. Obviously when they reached that percentage not much more money would be available from the banks for this purpose, and that is the situation in which the government finds itself today.
The banks had stopped lending and now they are being induced to increase lending for this purpose. We believe, of course, that the cost of housing will go up and as prices increase then the buyer of a house will really have to pay for it. The cost of money has gone up in the last few months by 20 per cent. Before the minister brought down the budget we advocated that certain steps should be taken, amongst them being the amending of Canada's banking legislation so as to channel savings deposits into longterm investments for uses such as housing, debenture and bond issues of municipalities, provinces, school and hospital boards.
We ask that action be taken similar to that taken in 1951 to defer depreciation

The Budget-Mr. A. Stewart allowances. We ask that corporations having a taxable income in excess of $20,000 and subject to standard corporation tax pay an immediate direct tax of 25 per cent imposed on their undistributed profits. We ask that legislation be brought in to regulate the volume of loans of finance companies, and we ask above all that this iniquitous measure should be repealed, namely, the provision of the Income Tax Act which permits a 20 per cent tax exemption on dividends from Canadian corporations. The government has done nothing whatsoever by fiscal means to reduce the threat of inflation and we are going to find as the months go on this year that the inflationary trend is still very much with us.
But while we are concerned with the effects of inflation and with the government's lack of policy, we are also very concerned with the absolutely inadequate measures taken by the government to improve substantially the position of the people of Canada in so far as social security is concerned. My friend, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), has got to take a major part of the responsibility because he accedes to these miserable pittances which are now being given to the Canadian people who demand and need very much more. My hon. friend has been a member of the government for many years. He is a believer in the free enterprise system. Were he working for a free enterprise company and had managed to fail so signally as he has failed here, he would have been fired long ago.
I think the best thing the minister can do in view of the failure of his policies is to get out and let somebody else handle the job who can do it.
Perhaps one reason for the failure of the minister is that he suffers from schizophrenia, he is not sure whether he is acting Secretary of State for External Affairs, or the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He has become thoroughly confused in those two jobs.
A little while ago he went to Asia at the request of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I am not sure whether he went there to act as a peripatetic record of his master's voice or as an advance agent for Chou-en-lai. It is debatable and anyone can make up his own mind about it. But I do know he has given a report on his journey. He tells us in this report that he saw the people dancing. I quote from his report of his visit to the Philippines as follows:
One of the highlights of this all too brief visit was the elaborate marienda dance which was performed for us by workers in the ministry of health.
I wonder what dance the workers in the ministry of health here might have performed for the minister when he came back. Perhaps they went through a ritualistic fire-dance in which I would have liked to have seen the minister take a very important part. You know, we have I.P.'s, meaning important persons; we have V.I.P.'s meaning very important persons; and we have V.I.P.I.'s meaning very important persons indeed.

There is an almost continuous settlement along the road for the 60 miles which separates Bogor from the capital. On hearing the strident noise of the siren of our police escort, people came out of their houses by the thousands to watch us pass. As I felt the occasion called for some manifestation of our friendship I waved continually to the crowd.
A great Canadian contribution to international friendship, a great Canadian contribution to the problems of the people of Indonesia. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget debate is of more than usual significance this year. In addition to the policy decisions of the government relating to fiscal matters, which it usually reveals, it also contains important announcements of government policy in respect of two items of veterans legislation and five items of social welfare legislation. The debate thus far has confined itself largely to discussions having to do with the matter of old age security and old age assistance. Completely overlooked is the provision announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) for disability pensions, for family allowances and for blindness allowances. Few have noted the importance of the government's effort during the past few months, in co-operation with the provinces, in the matter of a proposed nationwide
2608	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Martin scheme for hospital insurance, which I believe we are to discuss at the beginning of next week.
No one has mentioned that the total dollar value of the announcements made concerning social welfare by the Minister of Finance last week will come to some $132 million. When one thinks that our total responsibility dollarwise on federal account for old age pensions, before the universal scheme came into effect, was $100 million, and takes into account the fact that we are now proposing additions to present benefits totalling in all some $132 million, it will be seen that altogether apart from the commitment involved in hospital insurance, this government cannot on any count justifiably be accused by anyone in this house of not having taken the lead in the matter of social welfare legislation. This being a declaration, I recognize it should be supported by arguments, and that I now propose to do. Since these five items are all the administrative responsibility of the Department of National Health and Welfare, I propose to direct my attention to them particularly, rather than those other important matters referred to in my colleague's budget speech.
These five major changes, changes in social welfare policy, as announced in the budget were as follows: first, all pensioners 70 and over now receiving $40 a month under the Old Age Security Act will have their pensions raised effective July 1 of this year. The cost of this 15 per cent increase in the universal pension will amount to $60 million in the first year, well over half the total amount provided by the federal government in 1951, the last year of the former old age pension scheme. Now, family allowance payments in respect of children under six years of age, as well as of children who have passed their tenth but not their thirteenth birthday will be increased by one dollar monthly effective September 1 of this year. Incidentally, this family allowances program was first proposed by the present government of Canada at a time when it was not unanimously accepted in this house, and indeed in many quarters outside.
The increase in family allowance payments represents a total annual commitment of not less than $42 million a year. Now, this increase is equivalent to a 20 per cent increase in the amount of family allowance payments to younger children under six years of age and between 14 per cent and 15 per cent in the case of the older children, 10 to 13 years. An estimated 2.5 million children will benefit from the change in the $5 rate to $6, while an additional one million children will benefit


from the change in the $7 rate to $8. In addition to those groups who will derive immediate benefits effective September 1, a further 1.5 million children over six and under 10 years will likewise benefit when they reach their tenth birthday through the fact that they will receive a $2 increase in the rate of benefit instead of $1 as formerly. When hon. gentlemen attack these increases, let them consider what the total commitment is. It is $60 million for old age security, $42 million for family allowances, and that represents a very considerable expenditure of money, particularly when one takes into account that we are now spending over $400 million annually for family allowances in this country and close to $400 million on old age security. There is no country in the world that has a comparable record.
This means, Mr. Speaker, that five million children altogether out of 5.5 million on allowances will benefit from the increases announced last week by my colleague the Minister of Finance. This represents over 90 per cent of the children whose parents receive family allowances in the entire country. Only half a million children out of the 5.5 million, that is those who have passed their thirteenth birthday, will receive no added benefit but in a large number of cases these children have younger brothers and sisters and the family will thereby benefit. The cost of these benefits, as I say, will represent an additional $42 million to be borne by the taxpayers of Canada each year on top of the $412 million already shown in the main estimates as presented by the Minister of Finance. I think this is the proper place for me to make the observation that it is not the government that has to pay for these particular proposals; it is the people of Canada. It comes out of the hard work of the people of Canada and those hon. gentlemen on all sides of the house who do not bear this in mind are not fair in their presentation of this issue.
Now, with regard to old age assistance, the recipients of assistance under this legislation now number just over 90,000 people in our country. We share with the provinces on a fifty-fifty basis the cost of assistance on a means test basis up to a maximum of $40 a month. If the provinces agree, the federal government is now ready to enter into new agreements under which we will share the cost up to $46 a month. Action, of course, on this depends on the provinces.
Within a few hours of the delivery of the budget speech I telegraphed to all of the provincial governments and pointed out the decision of the federal government, and we are now awaiting for them to take the necessary legislative steps to make the agreements effective as soon as possible. A number of

the provinces have the legislative power to take advantage of our offer. In addition to increasing the maximum amount of assistance payable we are also proposing, if the provinces agree, to increase the over-all income ceilings as follows. And I would ask the house to note this and realize the significance of the amendments that are proposed. The income ceiling of a single recipient goes up from $720 to $840 a year; the income ceiling for a married recipient goes up from $1,200 to $1,320 a year; the income ceiling for a married recipient with a blind spouse goes up from $1,320 to $1,680 a year. We estimate that if all provinces agree to these changes the case load will rise from 90,000 recipients at present to about 95,000. The total additional costs will increase between 15 and 20 per cent, or slightly more than $8 million per annum. The federal share of this will be roughly $4 million.
With regard to disability allowances, no one in this house who has criticized the government, including the last speaker who spoke so amusingly, has mentioned the increase provided for disability allowances, and I am not aware that anyone in this house in this session or in the last session has ever asked the government to increase the basic amount of disability allowances.

With regard to disability allowances, it will be recalled that when the act was introduced I said we estimated that we would have a case-load of recipients of about 25,000. To give some indication of what the Disabled Persons Act means in terms of its effective results, I can now say that we have at the present time some 32,000 disabled persons on allowance, 7,000 more than we estimated. The proposed increase in the amount of the disability pension and in the income ceilings is exactly the same as in the case of old age assistance. In addition to this, however, we have proposed a new and more liberal definition of total and permanent disability to which nine of the provinces have now agreed. The effect of these changes will be to bring additional numbers of recipients on to the rolls. It is expected that by the end of the
The Budget-Mr. Martin fiscal year, 1957-58, the disability allowance cost load will have risen to a figure close to 40,000 recipients and, with the increase now contemplated, it will mean an increase in cost of about 15 to 20 per cent. The federal share of this will be about $1,500,000 a year.
When it is remembered that old age security and old age assistance take care of all persons in need over 65, including the disabled, that the blind and workmen's compensation and veterans' pension laws take care of other large numbers, that practically all institutional cases are excluded, any fair-minded person will agree, I am sure, that 32,000 to 40,000 disability pensioners is a high figure indeed to represent the totally and permanently disabled population between 18 and 65 in a country with Canada's economic prosperity and health facilities and general standard of health and well-being.
Little or nothing has been said about blindness allowances in this debate. No mention has been made of the fact that the government, through the Minister of Finance, has not only proposed a 15 per cent increase in the matter of disability allowances, old age assistance and old age security, but that we are doing something additional as well for the blind. I ask hon. gentlemen to compare what we have done for the blind in this country-the federal government, the provinces, the municipal governments and voluntary agencies together-with what other countries have done, and I can say with confidence that no one will be able to show me that in any other jurisdiction the measures are any more comprehensive than ours are. I do not mean by that that we have done all that we would like to be able to do, but I am saying that our legislation for the blind is comparable with that of any other jurisdiction. It will be recalled that while this is a sharing program, it is one that we bear to the extent of 75 per cent of the cost. The recipients of blindness allowance number 8,300 at the present time. As in the case of old age assistance and disability allowance, the federal government is proposing an increase in the maximum amount of pension payable from $40 to $46 monthly, and the increases proposed in the income ceilings are as follows. I give these to the house for the first time. Single blind person, from $960 to $1,080 per annum; single blind person with child dependent, from $1,160 to $1,560 per annum; married blind person with sighted spouse, from $1,560 to $1,680 per annum; married blind person with blind spouse, from $1,680 to $1,800 per annum.
What is the consequence of these changes? The consequence is that we now expect that the number of recipients of blindness

The Budget-Mr. Martin allowance will rise to 8,500, and that the annual cost will be increased by about $600,000 annually, of which $450,000 will be borne by the federal government.
A week ago I telegraphed to all the provinces-actually on March 15-communicating to them the details of the federal government's intentions and asking their concurrence. To date we have received affirmative replies from Manitoba, New Brunswick, Ontario and British Columbia. I have not yet received any definite reply by the way, from certain provinces, including the province of Saskatchewan. I have noted also from press reports of March 19 that the governments of Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia have announced their concurrence in the federal proposal. Interim acknowledgment has been received from Saskatchewan and Quebec has promised a further reply later on and I expect that shortly we shall hear from Alberta and Newfoundland.
I should also like to say a word about the size of the increase provided in relation to the increase in the cost of living since the Old Age Security Act and other acts were passed in 1952. The increases made compensate 71 times over for the increase in price levels since those laws were passed. Old age security payments were first made in January of 1952. Old age assistance payments to persons 65 to 70 years of age were first made in January of 1952. The new Blind Persons Act was also passed to take effect in January of 1952. Disability allowance payments were first made in January of 1955. In all of these acts the maximum amount of the pension was set at $40 in January 1952 or later.
If anyone would examine the situation and what has happened to the cost of living since 1952 he will see that the increase in the amount of pensions-15 per cent in its total effect-is very greatly in excess of the relatively slight increase that has taken place in the cost of living in that period.
I do not mind saying, as I said on another occasion, that to relate these benefits to the rise or decline in the cost of living or even to the gross national product can be a dangerous thing because if that standard is maintained at all times you could create a situation leading to pressure for reductions. Let no hon. member in this house fail to note that there is a demand for such reductions in many parts of this country through many of the newspapers which we read daily in this area, in this province and in the neighbouring province of Quebec.
One was drawn to my attention this morning which criticized the proposals we have made and which have been concurred in by


my colleagues with respect to social welfare benefit. I would simply like to say to those critics that while it is acknowledged that our welfare and health expenditures today on all accounts in Canada total about $1,850,000,000, the federal government being responsible for $1,500,000,000 of that,-and while these figures should be compared with the figure of $250 million in 1938 and represent a tremendous increase in the financial responsibility that governments have accepted in the matter of social welfare, nevertheless the health and social welfare policies and expenditures of this government represent, in terms of percentage and in relation to net national income and to the gross national product, a proportion of our national wealth and productivity that is no greater than it was in the year 1938.
That may give satisfaction to my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) but it is a complete answer to those people in the country who keep saying that this government is trying to establish in this country the welfare state. We are not seeking to establish the welfare state.
