speechtext:
When the Minister of National Health and Welfare was speaking a few moments ago he referred to the great contributions which the federal government makes to social welfare and he rather belittled the efforts of the provinces and the municipalities. It is not my intention to go into the reasons why the federal government should bear the greater burden in this regard. I think the reason is known to all members of the house and the people of the country generally.
As a matter of fact, whether it is federal, provincial or municipal taxes, it is the people of Canada who pay the bill. But if we make a comparison of the revenues received by the federal government and by the provincial and municipal governments across Canada we find that 78 per cent of the taxes are gathered by the federal government and 22 per cent by the provinces and municipalities. I think that answers very well why the responsibility is and should be placed on the shoulders of the federal government.
Just as an example, in 1956 federal government revenue increased 16 per cent according to the white paper issued by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), whereas the revenue of the provinces and municipalities increased by only 9 per cent. In that same year of 1956 federal expenses increased only 6 per cent whereas the expenses of the provinces and municipalities increased 13 per cent. I submit that that is a complete answer to the argument made by the minister a few moments ago about the burdens that should be borne by the federal, provincial and municipal governments.
Perhaps I can be pardoned this afternoon if I confine my remarks mainly to matters concerning the maritime provinces. The maritime provinces have come in for special attention in this budget. Apparently the federal government has at last discovered that there are maritime and eastern provinces in Canada. After 20 years of neglect, after the New Brunswick people realized that they were receiving nothing from this government and turned out their Liberal government in 1952, and gave them another sound trimming in 1955; after Nova Scotia which had had Liberal governments for most of the time since confederation realized that it had been neglected by this government and turned out its Liberal government in 1956, the federal government realized that the people of the maritime provinces were disgusted with the
The Budget-Mr. Brooks lack of attention which had been paid to them and their problems. We find by this budget that we are suddenly discovered by this government which is trying to make some amends for the neglect we have received at their hands over the last 22 years.
I have sat in this house and at times have heard our provinces referred to in a manner which 1 found to be humiliating. Our people of the maritime provinces are satisfied with most of the things down there. They are well satisfied with their climate and scenery. We feel there is no finer section in Canada in which to live than the maritime or eastern provinces. We are satisfied with our people, but there is one great exception.
That exception is the lack of a national policy. For the last number of years, and in fact almost since the days of confederation, there has not been a national policy in Canada which considered the rights of the people of these provinces. This is well illustrated by what is contained in the Gordon report which states that the income of the people of the maritime provinces is 37 per cent lower than the income of the people in the rest of Canada. I am not going to go into the history of how this situation has arisen because it has been referred to on many occasions. It is well known to all hon. members; it is well known to the government; it is well known to the people of Canada from one end to the other.
There are two things which have reacted particularly against the economic advancement of the eastern provinces, and both of these have been mentioned in the budget. One is the freight rates situation and the other is the lack of cheap electrical power. Those are two keys to the prosperity and success of our provinces. These are two matters which I contend have been neglected by this government now for many years.
The Gordon report mentioned the matter of freight rates. As I have just stated, it was not necessary for that to be mentioned in the Gordon report because it was well known. This situation has prevailed for a long time. If I had the time I could give a history of the freight rates situation in the maritime provinces since early days. Up until 1912, to put it briefly, we looked after our own freight rates and there was very little difficulty; but between 1912 and 1927 the situation kept getting gradually worse and there was an almost impossible situation existing at the time of the Duncan commission in 1927. At that time the recommendation was that something must be done and after that report was made the Maritime Freight Rates Act was put into operation.
Under the budget the government proposes a further examination of our transportation
2616	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Brooks system. It has been found that since 1927 the benefits which we receive under the Maritime Freight Rates Act have been gradually nullified and taken away. In 1946 railway experts in the maritime provinces examined the situation and found that practically all the benefits granted under the Maritime Freight Rates Act had been whittled down owing to the change in freight rates in Ontario and Quebec, and to a smaller degree in other parts of Canada. Because of the competition by trucks and water transport in Ontario and Quebec freight rates in those provinces were lowered while at the same time freight rates in the maritime provinces were raised. As a result, as I have just stated, all the benefits received under this act were nullified.
I am surprised that this is the year in which the Minister of Finance decides to bring about an improvement, as he calls it, in our situation. He should have acted ten years or more previously, but nothing has been done to relieve the situation until the budget of 1957.
What are we offered? We are offered $2 million as compensation for the lack of improvement in the freight rates situation in the eastern provinces. I said the other day, and I mentioned this briefly, that it is too little. I still contend that it is not realistic and does not meet the situation as far as our needs are concerned. In 1956 the amount paid under the Maritime Freight Rates Act was $14 million or 20 per cent of railway rates collected on freight moving west from the select territory under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. If $14 million represents 20 per cent of the western-bound freight, then the people in the select territory must have paid between $65 million and $70 million for freight that moved out of those provinces. It should be pointed out that the Maritime Freight Rates Act does not apply to freight moving from the west into the eastern provinces. The cost of the freight on all our automobiles, all the manufactured goods that come to New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland has to be absorbed in the price our consumers pay. The people of the maritime provinces not only pay between $65 million and $70 million for freight moving out of the province but I would say, although I have not the exact figures, that the cost of the freight coming into the eastern provinces would probably be another $65 or $70 million, making a total freight bill for these provinces of around $135 million or $140 million a year. We are now offered by this government a paltry sum of $2 million to offset our loss. I can assure the government that the people


of our province will realize that such an offer as this will not in any way improve the position of the maritimes. It will not introduce more industry into the provinces. This proposal means very little in paying the freight on goods going out of the province, and so far as freight coming into the province is concerned there is nothing at all provided.
When we are told that the government is being very generous in giving $2 million to assist in freight rates, I feel like using the expression which was used by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) when he said, "What is a million?". What is $2 million on a freight rate bill amounting to anywhere from $130 million to $150 million a year. I would venture to say that the cost of keeping three icebreakers on the St. Lawrence river-the Minister of Transport said the other day that it was two, but I checked and found it is three-for a month or five weeks in the spring to keep the ice clear in the gulf of St. Lawrence to advance a few weeks the opening of the port of Montreal comes to twice the $2 million that is paid to us on freight rates.
Now, Mr. Speaker, another matter which I mentioned a moment ago as being of great importance to our finances is cheap electric power. If we had these two matters cleared up, if we had low freight rates from our provinces so that our goods could compete in the markets of Canada with goods from other parts of the country, if we had cheap electric power which would encourage industry to come to our provinces and remain there, we could compete with any other province in Canada. The fact that we have not these things is the reason why the income of cur people is from 30 per cent to 37 per cent a year lower than the income of people in other parts of Canada. These are the reasons why our people are leaving our provinces and going to other parts of Canada. These facts have not been appreciated by this government until now, on the eve of an election. The Minister of Finance has suggested, as a solution to our power problem, certain proposals. It is too early for us to know just what effect the proposition might have on our electric power situation.
He suggests an interconnecting system between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and the introduction of thermal plants using coal from the two provinces but mostly from Nova Scotia. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that this is not a new idea. This is not an idea that has just been thought up by this government. The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacEachen) spoke about Professor Christie advocating this three or four years ago. At this stage I should like

"to ask the members from Nova Scotia, if this is such an excellent proposition to solve the power problems of the maritime provinces, why not one of them stood up in this house during the past three years and described it or advocated it to this house. Only a few months before an election do we hear any mention of it from any hon. member.
However, the government heard something about it, not from the members of the Liberal party and not from Professor Christie. When Premier Flemming of New Brunswick made his two propositions to the government for assistance in the development of power in the maritime provinces, particularly New Brunswick, his second or alternative proposition was along the lines of the one suggested by the Minister of Finance in his speech the other day. I should like to read, sir, from page 17 of the submission from the New Brunswick government presented to this government in January, 1956, for the development of electric power in New Brunswick particularly and in the maritime provinces generally. On page 17 the premier of New Brunswick has this to say, and this is an alternative proposition:
Or alternately,
(2) The government of Canada to advance to the government of New Brunswick the funds required for the projected construction program of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission through to March 31, 1967, the rate of interest to he that prevailing on long-term government of Canada bonds. As has been stated above, the funds required are estimated at $211,094,000.
Federal financial assistance on this scale would be a major contribution to the growth of the Atlantic region and the Canadian economy as a whole. It is of great importance to note that the large thermal units which it is proposed to erect in New Brunswick could provide a substantial market for New Brunswick and Nova Scotia coal, and provided a subvention was available to reduce the cost of coal to at least that of oil, calculated on a B.T.U. basis, the new market would be of the greatest assistance to the Nova Scotia coal industry which is beset by so many economic problems. The total coal requirements of these large thermal units is estimated at approximately 1,500,000 tons in 1965.
This was the submission presented by the premier of New Brunswick. You will note in that submission he not only mentioned using coal from the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia but he also suggested that the coal subventions should operate on coal used for electric power development as it does on coal going outside of Nova Scotia to other parts of Canada. I believe the subventions on Nova Scotia coal amount to about $6 million a year. We in the province of New Brunswick receive a few thousand dollars but most of our coal is consumed in the province. So far as subventions are concerned, we receive little benefit from them.
The Budget-Mr. Brooks
I should like to express this thought, that that was an alternative proposition made by the premier of New Brunswick. There are many matters which should be considered by the government in connection with this proposition and which should be thoroughly investigated. I have emphasized, and it has been emphasized many times, that the power we have in the maritime provinces must be cheap power. We can get lots of power from coal or from other sources, but unless it is cheap power, and the cheapest power we can get, it is of very little value as far as the introduction of industry is concerned. If power can be produced by this method cheaper than it can be produced from water resources, then I say, let us have it, but it must be thoroughly investigated.
We have talked about the production of power on the Saint John river. It has been investigated by the international joint commission; it has been investigated by some of the best hydro electric engineers in Canada. They all say it is a feasible proposition; they all say it is cheap, that we can get cheap power from that development if we can get the proper financial assistance. I suppose Great Britain has as much coal as any other small country in the world. As a matter of fact, she is sitting on a bottom of coal, but Great Britain today is studying the development of her electric power from atomic and nuclear energy. She has one plant in operation at the present time and five or six more are nearly completed, and now she is going to extend her activities to the building of 20 more plants. She claims that in 10 years time she can, through nuclear energy, produce cheaper electric power than it can be produced either by coal or by water resources.
When this is investigated, Mr. Speaker, we want to take all these factors into consideration. The premier of New Brunswick is anxious to use as much coal from New Brunswick and Nova Scotia as can be used, and we need to help our coal industry. The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond said this morning that this is going to be the gas pipe line for New Brunswick. The gas pipe line, Mr. Speaker, from which we received no benefit, is the reason that the coal mines of the province of Nova Scotia are having such a difficult time and have such a gloomy outlook for the future. Their markets have been taken away from them. Therefore, I do hope that if it is not possible to use complete thermo-electric power production, we may be able to use at least sufficient to help along these two industries in our different provinces. I say the matter should be thoroughly investigated. We in New Brunswick are very much hurt over the refusal of

The Budget-Mr. Brooks assistance for the Beechwood development. The people find it hard to understand why, when our provincial premier came to Ottawa for help, he was turned down. He realized the economic situation of our province; he realized the possibilities in that province for future development; he realized that we had natural resources which were comparable with practically any other province in Canada. He said he was determined that those natural resources would be produced and refined in our province. He is determined, if possible, to produce the electricity necessary for smelting and refining the minerals in our province, which is one of the poorest provinces in Canada financially. Finding it impossible to finance cheaply the operation and the building of a great dam on the Saint John river at Beechwood, which has since been completed but not without great cost and great anxiety on the part of the government and the people, he approached the federal government in Ottawa and asked for assistance. He did not ask the federal government to give money to the province of New Brunswick but to lend money with the borrowing strength of the federal government behind it. The money could have been borrowed at a cheap rate of interest.
He and the people of New Brunswick were turned down. Just a few months afterwards -you have heard this story often but, as I say, the people of the province of New Brunswick fail to understand it-when a United States company wished to build a pipe line from Alberta to Toronto and Montreal to supply gas, and when money was plentiful almost anywhere in Canada or the United States for this purpose, this government felt that it had to assist in the building of the pipe line, but it refused absolutely to help the province of New Brunswick in a matter which would have meant very much to the future prosperity of that province.
This is something which the people of my province find very difficult to understand. I would like to read part of the submission that was made to the federal government at that time with reference to assistance for the development of hydro electric power at Beechwood. At page 4 of the submission sent by the premier to the government he had this to say:
At prevailing costs for provincial financing, approximately 5 per cent, capital expenditures on such a scale would represent a heavy burden calculated to have adverse effects upon the credit position of New Brunswick. The estimated cost of delivered energy in mills per kilowatt hour would be 6.92 for 5 per cent money, 4.76 mills for 21 per cent money.
It was believed that it would cost the province 5 per cent on the money that they obtained to develop this hydro electric power.


It was believed that, with the assistance of the federal government, the money could be obtained for 2J per cent, and, as is stated here, the difference in mills per kilowatt hour would be 6.92 for 5 per cent money as compared with 4.76 mills for 2J per cent money, a difference of over 2 mills per kilowatt hour, which is, I might say, just the difference between costly and cheap electric power. That is the situation.
The submission goes on to say:
It can be seen that borrowings at present rates will only accentuate the problem of high-cost power.
As I mentioned a moment ago, my province was not asking that this money be given to it. A proposition was submitted by which the money would be paid back, and on page 5 of the submission we find:
That repayments be made at the rate of 1.5 per cent of the principal amount each year; the first payment to be due one year after the completion of the particular project for which the money was advanced.
I mention these things, Mr. Speaker, to show that we have been very sadly neglected by this present government. I think the people of my province will look askance at these deathbed efforts, I might say, these last minute efforts just before an election. We hope that they are serious. We hope that something will be done, but the government had its opportunity. In my opinion this country of ours has the most out of balance economy in the world. The economic policy of Canada has been so built up as to allow the centre of this dominion to have most of the manufacturing industries, with people coming particularly from the east to find opportunities here. Everything has been done for the central part of Canada and the other parts of the country have been neglected.
I have compared in this house before and I compare again the attitude which is taken by the government of the United States. We all know that following the civil war the southern states shipped all their cotton to the northern states. Their economy was depressed and the people were poor. I believe it was Mr. Roosevelt who a few years ago said that all parts of the United States should have equal opportunities. In the southern states hydroelectric power has been developed through the Tennessee valley association.

Thank you; the Tennessee valley authority. That was not done by the state of Tennessee or by any of the southern states. It was done by the federal government at Washington. The result has been that the southern states have become a great manufacturing section of that country. Their

people are staying there and they are finding work. Tremendous industrial development has taken place.
The same thing has occurred in the northwestern part of the United States. I read only the other day in a newspaper article that the Dakotas, another somewhat depressed area in the United States, are receiving attention from the federal government at Washington. I have in my hand a report from Sioux Falls, South Dakota, dated March 5, 1957. The article reads:
There has been an increase of 64 per cent in the power generated this past year by the four dams built on the Missouri river by the federal government.
I emphasize the words "by the federal government". The article continues:
Despite this growing influx of power, it has been announced that an atomic power plant-*
In addition to hydroelectric power they are developing an atomic power plant. I observe that the minister smiles at the suggestion of an atomic power plant. I believe it is atomic power plants that will save the economy of Great Britain and they could very well save the economy of certain parts of Canada, too. The article continues:
Despite this growing influx of power, it has been announced that an atomic power plant, adding millions of more kilowatts of electricity to present sources, will be built in or near the Sioux Falls area by Northern States Power Company.
I commend to this government the attitude of the government of the United States. If our federal government want to make this country of ours one great nation, if they want to have people remain in their homes in all sections of the dominion, and if they want the maritimes to prosper-and we have everything there except cheap electric power and cheap transportation-then they will have to adopt an attitude similar to that adopted by the United States government. In my opinion the maritime provinces could prosper as well as any other part of this country.
I would like to mention a few of the opportunities which this government have had to assist the maritimes. They have taken this opportunity of granting assistance just before the election but I would like to point out some of the opportunities they have had during the past 20 years or more. I have already mentioned the Beechwood project and I shall say nothing more about it at this time. It is well known to everyone that we were turned down with respect to the Beechwood project.
For many years we have been advocating the construction of a canal across the Chig-necto isthmus. This has been advocated for many years in this house. I see that the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) is in his
The Budget-Mr. Gregg seat. It has certainly been advocated ever since he and I came to this house and for many years before that.
I believe that the Chignecto canal is probably needed more today than at any time in the history of the maritime provinces. In speaking about it in this house a few years ago I said that it was complementary to the development of the St. Lawrence seaway. Anyone who looks at the map of eastern Canada and sees the routes that coastal ships have to take away around the northern part of Nova Scotia in order to reach Saint John or Portland or any of the eastern Atlantic ports will realize that a canal through this narrow neck of land some 16 miles across would assist greatly in the development of water transportation in that area.
Some people have expressed the opinion that the St. Lawrence seaway is being developed because United States interests in Labrador needed to facilitate the transportation of iron ore from Labrador and northern Quebec.
The United States coastal shipping industry would benefit from the Chignecto canal and if it is pressed for by them I feel that possibly we will have a better chance of getting it than if the people of the maritime provinces alone request it. We have pressed for it for many years and I believe it will now be asked for not only by the people of the maritimes but also by the coastal shipping industry of the United States. Their ships could pass through it and through the St. Lawrence and down into the great lakes.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have this chance to follow my friend the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) in a discussion of the budget. Friday afternoon is probably a very good time for a discussion of the province of New Brunswick and its affairs to be brought before this house, and I for one am extremely anxious that this subject should be brought forward this afternoon in a thoughtful fashion, in a fair fashion, and without attempts to utilize any features of New Brunswick need as a political football or as a matter of partisan discussion.
I am going to say immediately that I welcomed the note of optimism that I discerned in the voice of my hon. friend today. I also welcomed the commendation-reserved though it was, but still wholehearted-the hon. member gave this government for the actions it has taken. But when he was comparing the percentage of revenue raised by

The Budget-Mr. Gregg federal, provincial and municipal governments during the fiscal year 1955-56 the hon. member forgot to mention that this government, as I shall point out later in my remarks, collected from the taxpayers of Canada and spent in his and my province of New Brunswick in that year a total of $127 million.
During that same year and because of the amounts that were so spent, the province of New Brunswick found it necessary to raise by direct provincial taxation and by sundry revenues such as the sale of liquor and from other sources less than $30 million to meet the provincial budget.
The hon. member has commended the federal government for taking action on what he describes as the two most important and needed factors in our Atlantic region economy -and I wholly agree with him in this- cheap power and cheap transportation. He said that immediate action for increasing the subsidy on outgoing freight does not meet the situation in so far as transportation is concerned. I quite agree with that, because if it did meet the situation there would have been no cause for this government to take the second and more important step of complying with the recommendations of the Gordon commission and indeed in complying with the recommendations of the transportation committee of the maritimes board of trade, which it has done in both cases.
He said further that if these two matters were cleared up we could, indeed, compete with the rest of Canada. I may not go with him the whole way on that. I think we would have to have some other things, but I think in general I agree. I am not going at this time to enter into a technical and financial discussion regarding power, but I think there is an impression that should be cleared up now. The brief that came to this government in January, 1956, from which the hon. member quoted, quite clearly indicated a budget reflecting the power thinking of that time. There was a total budget of $211 million. Now the impression has been gained-how, I will not discuss-that Beechwood and its ramifications is requiring or will require a great slice of that $211 million. I know my hon. friend did not attempt to give that impression today, but it has been given elsewhere.
As a matter of fact the first phase of Beechwood is to cost approximately $15 million and the second phase will carry the cost, which is still in the future, up another $15 million to a total of $30 million. The third phase is still in abeyance; the experts are still talking about it.


Mr. Speaker, the budget gives me a chance to bring to the attention of the house some special things related to my native province that I have often wanted to discuss here. Though representing a constituency and a province which are in the main rural, much of my time has been related to the industrial centres of our country and to those who work there. For a while now I want to speak on behalf of the rural workers of my section of Canada.
In early years on a hilltop farm I knew intimately the New Brunswick rural scene of that period as did the hon. member for Royal. In later years, after some vicissitudes, it has been interesting to have a part in the surge and stress of the industrial centres of Canadian activity. The memories of the surroundings of my youth are still fresh, the more so because I have the chance to visit them often. This being the case, I have an understanding of my fellow Atlantic region residents, who looked with a jaundiced eye at that minor part of the Gordon commission report that had to do with deportation. However, that initial irritation did cause many people, who otherwise might not have done so, to study the report.
I like to think I have learned something of the aims and aspirations of those who labour on the New Brunswick hillsides as well as those who work in the more noisy and crowded communities of our country. As long as I am a member of the government from New Brunswick, with this portfolio, I feel I have some responsibility for the well-being of both.
For the latter, the industrial workers, highly organized channels exist through which their wishes can be made known to government at all levels. For the former it is not so easy. At the time of confederation, in the areas of New Brunswick outside the cities and towns, there were 9 persons per square mile. Today there are 14 persons per square mile. As the tempo of population growth is known on this continent, that cannot be called rapid.
Those who do remain there are not there because they are stranded but because they have chosen to remain, or to return after some time of absence. Why have they so chosen? They have done so because they believe they get from life there the things they want to a greater degree than they can elsewhere. It is perhaps not surprising that many have gone west and south from New Brunswick. Far pastures always look greener; people are ever impressed by the attractions of places where people live together in large numbers. Expatriates-and there are many in various parts of the world who come from

New Brunswick-often send back to the folks at home more glowing reports than their conditions warrant. Statistics tell how much higher salaries and wages are in central Canada or in New England or British Columbia than they are in New Brunswick.
But statistics do not tell the whole story; there are compensations. Down where I come from in the country, most people who work get their meals at home. They live and work in healthy surroundings, they have a personal and family privacy, and most of them know everybody else in the community. Most of them, too, enjoy the attractions of the woods, the hills and the sea. Some of them can still catch a few speckled trout near home- sometimes the hon. member for Royal poaches in my waters-and they all know that their neighbour judges them by their industry and integrity, not by the size of their fixed assets or bank accounts.

speechtext:
As long as the hon. member doesn't tell the house I shall not mind.
Such a life makes for simplicity. Simplicity is less expensive than complexity. Besides, it is easier on the nervous system and much more pleasant as a way of living. To say that rural New Brunswick will never become a replica of southwestern Ontario is not to cry with the voice of jealousy or of despair, neither is it crying down the real attractions of the big urban areas.
Few will deny the pull of life in the large cities. There is great diversity. There is variety of social relationships, of entertainment, of educational and cultural opportunities. To me one of the atttractive features of Canada's big urban areas is that they send here members who cordially support measures that will help the rural worker of the Atlantic provinces. As a New Brunswicker I would like to see more of the kind of economic strength that has made our urban areas in central Canada big and available as an economic foundation for the kind of country life we want to retain and develop in New Brunswick under our own power.
This is not just so we may also be big and crowded. It is that we might create opportunities for those who now go away but who would rather stay there and live their lives and raise their families. Many of the items that are contained in this year's budget will do much toward helping to gain this objective. They are designed so to do.
In years past there has been pessimism as to whether we would ever be able to 82715-166
The Budget-Mr. Gregg strengthen the economic foundation and find the opportunities. More recently, while a few of the briefs on New Brunswick submitted to the Gordon commission showed some hope, there has been a tendency to look with concern upon the gloomy side. In its turn, the Gordon report found a good deal of evidence for good cheer in the natural resources which are available to be conserved and developed.
They found problems, too, and the report did not blink when it came to those problems. There were the problems of the submarginal farms, of transportation, of resource development, of education, of fostering and encouraging existing basic and secondary industries and finding scope for new ones. I am very glad that the commission faced these Atlantic problems with deep concern rather than by just saying that everything in our garden was lovely. The commission made some hints and some speculations and some very good and firm recommendations. I say with a good deal of satisfaction that the federal government has already announced in the budget and otherwise its determination to carry out the spirit of several valuable suggestions in the report having to do with the Atlantic provinces.
Having to some extent charted the course of the battle against defeatism in the Atlantic area, I wonder whether it was a very sinful thing for the commission to face facts and admit that there still might be some casualties who should be given help to go to a better place in which to recuperate. In cooperation with several of the provinces we in my department have been providing financial help to willing Canadians who could get no work where they were, to enable them to go where work could be found. The Gordon report felt this might be continued and perhaps extended where absolutely necessary. That to my mind is not deportation. It is the practical application of an effective and necessary placement plan.
Quite a few things have been going on in recent years that are having good effects upon our rural countryside down east. Our No. 1 industry in New Brunswick is the woods industry. These resources are under the exclusive jurisdiction of the province. Nevertheless, the federal government has realized the importance of the survival of this industry to our country people, and has been assisting financially in the cost of a long-term inventory. It has been sharing the cost of what has now become quite a long-term and hard-fought battle to halt- the devastation by insects in our forest areas, and it is costing a lot of federal money. Last

The Budget-Mr. Gregg year a further step was taken by sharing in the cost of fire protection by an amount that will be approximately a quarter of a million dollars in New Brunswick during the next five years.
While this action to defeat the twin forest enemies of bug and fire reacts mainly, I think, to the benefit of the pulp and lumber industry, it is also an important conservation factor for many individual farmers as well, because the average farm in New Brunswick is made up of one portion of crop land and pasture and the other portion of wood lot. To protect the forest and the farm wood lots the federal government on its own account and at its own expense has set up scientific services and facilities at the University of New Brunswick, at Mount Allison University, at the provincial experimental farm and at Acadia forestry station, and on all these activities related to forests, some of which react to the benefit of the farms, the federal government expended in New Brunswick in 1955-56 a total of over $1 million.
This, of course, brings me to another of our New Brunswick methods of attempting to earn a living in the rural areas; that is, farming. Very often farming as the main effort is augmented by lumbering, by pulp cutting either on or off the farm, by fishing- 1 mean fishing for fish to sell-by construction work, or by guiding sportsmen, or by a combination of one, two or three of the activities I have mentioned. As indicated recently by the Prime Minister-and I like to think he was talking about the small, 120-acre more or less Atlantic province farm -the situation on these small eastern farms has reached the point where it must receive very special federal attention and study. So we have working in the other place a committee which is doing just that. I am glad it is conducting this inquiry, and I hope it will find some good solutions for the small farmers about whom I am talking today.
Some may think that because I am Minister of Labour I have no particular interest in agriculture, but that is not true. The economic welfare of our country homes and the morale of the people who work there have a tremendous impact upon the well-being of our whole Canadian life in general and the industrial workers in particular. My department has to do with the activities of labour in the broadest sense. We cover all members of the Canadian working force including the farmer, the farmer's family and the hired man. Through its farm labour program my department and the national employment service co-operate with the federal and provincial departments of agriculture and other interested bodies in helping to meet seasonal and year-round farm labour needs.


I have spoken of this program generally at other places and I will do so again. However, it is of value mainly to the large commercial agriculturist for whom I have great respect and regard but about whom I am not talking today. I am speaking here about the conditions prevailing on the little farms of my province, most of which can afford neither heavy farm equipment nor any great amount of hired help.
Here is where the federal social security measures that were outlined by the Minister of Finance in the budget and explained by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in his address this afternoon come into play. It is in these areas that we get such tremendous value from the federal social security measures as a backlog of security. One point to remember about the people on these farms is that even though they have little income, many do obtain genuine satisfaction from the basic values inherent in rural life. There is a danger perhaps of these simple yet real values of farm life being lost when agriculture becomes very highly commercialized. On the other hand, I think it is possible to improve the country workers' economic position in my part of the country without losing these basic values. There should be no conflict, in other words, between agriculture as a way of life and agriculture as a mere means of earning a livelihood.
It must be recognized, however, that on their own it is not easy for these farm families to improve their economic position. It may be that their farm is too small for efficient operation, or that the soil is too poor. These are factors that will be explored by the Senate committee on agriculture. They may be too far from a market. In this regard I hope the steps indicated in the budget will help, namely the increase in the freight subsidy on products shipped out, and the new look at how all the means of transportation may be improved. While these studies are under way, the important work being done on a regular basis by the federal and provincial departments of agriculture on soil surveys, on crop and livestock improvement and on other types of experimental work will be continued, and I am sure will eventually be integrated into the main effort. In much the same way facilities have been made available in New Brunswick for the encouragement of the farmer wood lot owner so he may get the best long-term value from the wooded portion of his farm.
I speak with great conviction on these matters because I have seen the value of having as part of our Veterans Land Act administration field men well qualified in farming methods to assist farmer veterans on a regular month to month basis to organize

and develop their little farms. I believe that much of the success of this effort has been due to the continuity of the guidance and to the practical application of scientific knowledge. I hope that plan, too, and how it has developed will be taken into account in the co-ordinated study that is now going on.
More attention is also needed with respect to the capital and the training required today, especially by our young farmers in the light of the high cost of land and of mechanization, and the improvements that are taking place in farming methods. The greater capital that is needed in this regard has been recognized this session by the improvement of our federal farm loan act brought in by the Minister of Finance.
The Department of Labour co-operates with the provinces, including my own, in the training of farm youth, just as we have done in other industries, and this year I have in my estimates the means for extending this type of training. I think training in this context should not be confined to the learning of new techniques. Even though the economic farm unit of the future must be larger and even if, as the Gordon report says, relatively fewer people will be on the farms, nevertheless we ought to help our people who will work there to seek richer and fuller lives.
In that field, without thinking of any government particularly, one cannot help but think of the useful efforts that are being made in the broader educational field by such organizations as 4-H clubs, which are of great assistance to young people in the country, and by that grand group of country organizations the women's institutes-which are located all across Canada. There are helpful things economically that the federal government has been doing, such as the subsidy on feed grain, floor prices on the dairy products which have been referred to most recently, the maritime freight rate subsidy which has been discussed, the marshlands reclamation, the lime program, and other things.
To encourage production and to stabilize year-round distribution in the provinces the federal government has assisted in the capital cost of public cold storage plants, and has given encouragement to co-operative plans of one kind and another. One cannot leave the farming picture in New Brunswick without stressing the importance of our own Atlantic provinces home market, which is growing. Another is the importance of good transportation facilities to central Canada, which has been discussed.
Recent developments are augmenting the home market. The five cities and perhaps a score of towns in New Brunswick, even though they are not large, offer the best 82715-166i
The Budget-Mr. Gregg possible markets for our country products. These urban centres are growing. Camp Gagetown and the town of Oromocto, where a total of $100 million will have been expended federally by 1958 by the Minister of National Defence and by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, will be a continuing market for farm products, for there will be an additional 15,000 population of men, women and children during the years ahead. In this and other ways this project has been giving to our New Brunswick community the greatest economical lift I think it has had for a long time. To this is mainly due the fact that in New Brunswick this last year we have had the nearest thing to full employment that we have had since the far away days of wooden ships and iron men.
I should like to refer briefly again to the Maritime Freight Rates Act, referred to by the hon. member for Royal. Since 1927 this act has been of great assistance to the shippers of agricultural products to central Canada, but gradually the benefits have been whittled down because of the increase in freight rates. The present plan will raise the subsidy from 20 per cent to 30 per cent on outgoing shipments, and will be of great assistance.
But that is not the whole story. There is the further plan of complying with the recommendation of the Gordon commission to conduct a thorough-going investigation into all phases of transportation, rail, water, air and, by co-operation with the province, road. This holds good hope for the future, and I know all our people in New Brunswick will welcome it.
Joining with the province of New Brunswick, or acting on its own in promoting activities designed for the improvement of our farming industry, the federal government expended in 1955-56, the last fiscal year for which records are complete, approximately $4.5 million.
The tourist business offers great possibilities. I have long felt that our province could develop its resources to the maximum and at the same time retain and improve the unspoiled features of our countryside, a welcome retreat for people during the open season. I could tell you much about the attractions of our New Brunswick air-conditioned Fundy national park, but the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will do that quite ably, I know, when he presents his estimates. Incidentally, I should like to thank him for the interest he has taken in the park as well as in the development of our resources generally. This park is becoming increasingly popular, and it pleases me very much that this is the case not only with visitors but with our own people as well.

The Budget-Mr. Gregg
It gives me satisfaction to know that in this coming year, in addition to all the regular federal tourist advertising, the Atlantic provinces have a special budget for this purpose of $300,000 under the federal tourist bureau. This new and larger advertising program will prove most useful. Its success will be helped by federal co-operation in building the Trans-Canada highway and in subsidizing transportation across to the great island in the gulf of St. Lawrence, Prince Edward Island. One of the many advantages that we in New Brunswick have in being a neighbour of the island is the fact that nearly all the many thousands of tourists who visit the island must pass back and forth across New Brunswick in order to do so.
Until a few years ago we thought we had no base metals in New Brunswick, but in the late 1940's the provincial government undertook an investigation, in the course of which the federal government co-operated in carrying out an airborne magnetometer survey of the northern part of the province. Out of that survey there emerged directly the realization that New Brunswick had a mineralized area which placed it among the leading mining regions of Canada. By the very nature of things our country people, about whom I am talking, have not taken any large part in putting up the risk capital required, so they have not had much part in the paper profits that have been made nor will they participate greatly in future dividends. This is true even though this provincial natural resource is the property of all the people of the province. It is true because our country people have not the money with which to speculate.
However, I hope the processing of these minerals will be carried out to the most advanced stage possible within our province. Even in this technological age this processing will provide employment for a number of our workers. But there is another phase. In addition to the fruits of speculation and of employment there are the important fruits of the production royalties which will accrue to the provincial government.
Here is where I hope the fruits of this mining development will be felt, and really felt, in the well-being of our people. You may ask how. It will be. by augmenting provincial revenues so that provincial taxation may be less; by making more revenue available for schools, roads, health, and all those things which go to make for a higher standard of living about which we have been talking. I hope the provincial government is now enacting measures so our own people will in fact receive a fair dividend from the exploitation of their own provincial resources.
Before I leave this topic I want to thank the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys

for having carried out a new airborne magnetometer survey across the southern part of New Brunswick, and for the increased tempo of geological parties working this area this summer. When this survey is completed I am sure many people down there will be anxious to use the results.
I should like to pay a special tribute to the courage, industry and perseverance of the fisher-folk along our Fundy and gulf shores. They have proved indeed the hardihood of our New Brunswick population. That is why I hope some real value may accrue to them, as well as to fishermen all over Canada, when unemployment insurance begins to function next year as far as they are concerned.
The Department of Fisheries has been conducting an aggressive program on behalf of these producers. There is a fishing bounty which is designed to aid them. There is assistance to the fishermen in the form of educational work in co-operative producing and selling. There is assistance in the form of industrial development for technical services. There is construction assistance for fishing vessels. There is assistance to bait freezers for fishermen. There is insurance of fishermen's boats and gear against loss by storm.
I can truthfully say that more helpful programs for our fishermen have been put under way during the last 10 years than during the whole period before that since confederation. Fisheries is a federal responsibility, and last year the Department of Fisheries expended over a million dollars to improve the conditions of our fishermen in New Brunswick.
No survey of the economic strengthening of New Brunswick would be at all complete without some reference to the federal-New Brunswick tax sharing arrangement or agreement. The simple fact is that this sharing of tax moneys with the continuing equalization feature is New Brunswick's foundation for hope of economic improvement or salvation, and also for real Canadian unity as we see it down there. Ten years ago, in 1945-46, at the beginning of the tax agreements, the federal government on all accounts provided the provincial treasury of New Brunswick with approximately $6 million from Canadian taxpayers at large. During the year 1955-56 the transfer on all accounts from Ottawa to Fredericton was $42 million, made up of $18.5 million from tax rentals and $23.5 million in health grants, social security payments, trans-Canada highway, vocational training and these other things. In addition the federal government departments and agencies spent in New Brunswick, directly to individuals or in communities,

a total of $85 million in 1955-56. So I think my hon. friend from Royal will immediately agree that the dear old province has not been so badly neglected as he tried to indicate this afternoon.

Along with the $127 million in federal tax money that were expended in New Brunswick, there was less than $30 million collected from New Brunswick being spent by the provincial government. There was something less than $54 million in direct and indirect taxes collected from New Brunswickers by the federal treasury in 1955-56, included in which are all the import and customs revenues from the constituency of my hon. friend the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, from the great port of Saint John.
Why do I bring in these fiscal totals in a talk on behalf of people in the New Brunswick rural areas? I can tell my hon. friends it is not in any sense of the word a political motive that urges me on. I do so because in some quarters, and I shall not stop to mention them, statements have been made to create the impression amongst these same hard-working people that this federal government is not trying to encourage their efforts. These statements are absolutely false. The people of our province have constantly added to the wealth of the corporations of central Canada from whom much of the equalization money originates. The large sums I have mentioned are in no sense of the word hand-outs. They are evidence of the willingness of this government to see to it that some of Canada's wealth goes back to the people at the ends of the country who help to earn it, which lays a sound foundation for Canada's unity and good will, and this our people will ever remember.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have just listened to the minister telling how much the government put into some provinces and how much they may have taken out. It goes without saying that if the government puts into one province more than it takes out.
262G	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Hansell then it must take out of some other province more than it puts in. There may not be anything wrong with that. Perhaps it is just logical to assume that some of the wealthier provinces may, at times, have to act as a sort of big brother to some of the less wealthy provinces.
A few nights ago, Mr. Speaker, we listened to what was supposed to be an election budget. After the speech had been delivered by the Minister of Finance one of my colleagues came to me and said, "I do not think that is an election budget; if you ask me, it is a sort of an election dud." I thought I knew what "dud" meant but I took Webster's dictionary and purposely looked up the meaning of the term. I found that the definition was "a thing that does not go off". If the minister's budget was an election budget, I am afraid they will find it is a dud, because I do not think it will go off with the people of Canada as anything to be proud of when they begin to realize the vast wealth that Canada possesses.
I would characterize the budget as one without imagination. Canada is a country rich in mineral and oil resources, rich in all sorts of natural resources; huge forests; vast farmlands; vast wheat and grain producing areas; oceans to the east and west teeming with fish; power galore; coal mines that can produce coal for generation upon generation to come. Yet we find that this same coal mining industry is in the most deplorable and depressed condition of any industry in the country. When we look to this present government for a solution of those problems, particularly the problem of the coal mining industry, I declare that they have not got a clue.
We have the possibility of vast storages of water, yet we have to argue over the Saskatchewan dam. The hon. member for Acadia has suggested over and over again a plan in respect of the Red Deer diversion project. But these projects are not developed. Why? Because the budgetary proposals of the finance minister year in and year out have no imagination. No new proposals are enunciated that can be applied to the real problems which face this nation. It is a budget with little concept of reality.
What is needed in Canada is a change in financial policy that will take the bull by the horns and make that which is physically possible and desirable financially possible. We have heard orthodox ministers of finance use that term, copying it from the Social Crediters. Oh, yes, they would make that which is physically possible and desirable financially possible, but we wait year in and year out and find no such change in financial policy.


Not so long ago I was talking to a top newspaper man, one of considerable repute, who said to me, "You know, I never have been able to quite understand your Social Credit monetary proposals". And he ended his few sentences by saying, "It does not matter to me, Mr. Hansell, what you propose in changing any financial policy. You have to use the same deck of cards; you cannot come along and use some other deck of cards". So I turned to him and said, "Well, now, whoever told you that we were going to use another deck of cards?" He said, "Well, that is my way of putting it; it is a metaphor that I am using". I said, "No, that is where you are wrong; we would use the same deck of cards but we would change the rules of the game, and we would change them in such a way that the people would have a chance once in a while at least of winning the jackpot".
I think what is needed in Canada today, Mr. Speaker, is an alternative financial policy to that which this government has been proposing over the last 21 years. I have sat in this house and listened to 21, if not more, annual budgets, and still they come down with no new policies enunciated. Oh, they may boost taxation here and reduce it there; they may try to balance their books. Finance ministers come and finance ministers go, but their job year in and year out is only a matter of seeing how much they can get when they bleed the people and how much they can spend after bleeding them, and it does not take very much brain power to figure that out. In my mind there is nothing imaginative in anything of that kind. What we need is an alternative to the present financial policy and I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the Social Credit party of this country presents that alternative.
It is a significant thing, Mr. Speaker, that the only two Social Credit governments in Canada are beginning to reverse the order, and instead of taking something from the people are beginning to give the people something back.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There are only two Social Credit governments in the world and they do not practise Social Credit; that is the strange thing about it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know whether my hon. friend's remarks got on Hansard, but if those two provinces can do what they are doing without the adoption of Social Credit monetary policies, imagine what they could do if they could adopt Social Credit monetary policies, if they had the constitutional right to do it. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, put a Social Credit government in Ottawa where we will have the constitutional authority in terms of currency, credit and banking, and then see

what can be done in this country. Then see whether or not we can develop our coal mining areas; then see whether we can develop our forests and the wealth of our natural resources. I think it is almost beyond imagination what we could do if we adopted a proper financial policy.
The government of British Columbia decided to return something to the people of that province and they returned it by alleviating the tax burden, giving it to the people and saying, "This will help you to pay taxes on your homes". That is something worthy of note. When the Alberta government began to calculate their income from the oil industry in the past year they turned around and they said, "The natural resources of the province belong to the people. It is only right that they should share in those natural resources". They took part of the oil royalties which came in as revenue to the province and said, "We are going to give our citizens a dividend from those oil royalties". They are now passing legislation whereby everyone over 21 will receive a cash dividend from part of the revenue they receive from their oil royalties.
Now, of course, as soon as a government reverses the order and, instead of taking something away from the people, begins to give something to the people, something they can handle with their own hands and spend on things of their own choice, the cry goes up from politicians, from Liberal and Conservative newspapers, "Oh, that is morally wrong; you should never do that". Now, imagine saying it is morally wrong to give to the people part of that which is their own natural heritage. Even the Minister of Labour, when referring to his own province this afternoon, declared that the natural resources belong to the people. Well, now, should it be morally wrong to return to the people something that is their perfect right to share in?
When I say the Liberal and Conservative press cries to high heaven and tries to portray a moral wrong that exists in this situation, I must admit that not all the newspapers have joined in the same cry. My attention has been drawn to an article in the Camrose Canadian which is a splendid weekly newspaper published in the very fine town of Cam-rose. I think it is more than a town; it is becoming a young city. The people of Cam-rose are to be congratulated on their fine weekly newspaper, just as they are to be congratulated on the representative they sent to this house, who came here as the result of a by-election held not very long ago. He has really come to grips with the problems that face his constituents, and is one of the most active members in this house.
The Budget-Mr. Hansell
Let me return to the Camrose Canadian. Here is what it says about the action of the government of Alberta in returning to the people a part of their heritage:
There were several factors In the new Alberta budget, brought down by the provincial treasurer, Hon. Mr. Hinman, that could have been pounced upon for criticism by the political opponents, but that $22 direct dividend cheque was not one of them. Even there it is very evident that the idea embraces a good deal of political expediency . . . but it's mighty potent expediency. Had the dividend come out of general taxation revenues we would have laid into the ethics of the move ourselves, but this money is direct oil royalty money-money derived from natural resources, more or less a legacy. Our only criticism is that the dividend was not set at a higher figure, say $50 per adult. Thus Alberta is doing something no other province in Canada has ever been able to do . . . directly distribute some fruits of the natural resources to the people. Most people will welcome the chance to spend this money as they see fit.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the cries against such a policy wail forth from the politicians not because they think it is wrong, even though they may say that, but because they know it is a reversal of the outworn policies of old line governments, and because it begins to sound the death knell of the old political parties in this country.
Nothing is said concerning moral wrong when a government hands out cheques in the form of family allowances, and no mention is made of anything being morally wrong when a government doles out pension cheques to people who are incurably ill or in the form of veterans allowances, all of which we support. When a billion dollar oil company issues its annual dividends as the result of profitable investments, no cry goes up as to the moral wrong in that case. If people buy stock in an oil company and as a result of having that stock receive a yearly dividend, there is no cry of moral wrong. When a person deals in leases and sells them and receives in return stock in the company and an annual dividend, no one says there is anything morally wrong in that. If a farmer who settled on a homestead prior to 1905 has oil rights on his land and sells them to an oil company, and receives stock and dividends which cause him to become a very wealthy man, no cry goes up about there being anything morally wrong in that and we do not say there is. But when the Social Credit government through their careful administration are able to obtain revenue from a natural resource which belongs to the people, and turn around and say, "Now, we are able to give you a little share in this natural resource," the politicians shout to the high heaven that it is morally wrong.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, I have not yet heard one politician say he will go out on any election platform or issue in any printed political platform a statement to the effect

The Budget-Mr. Hansell that if he is voted into office he will withdraw that dividend from the people and channel it in some other way, giving it back in the form of municipal grants for roads, hospitals, health benefits or anything else. I have not heard one politician say he would go out on that sort of platform.
I want to call to your attention another small matter in respect to this dividend which I think is a shame. Of course someone had to rise and ask the Minister of National Revenue whether this cash gift from the governments of British Columbia and Alberta to the people of those provinces would be considered income and therefore taxable for income tax purposes, and of course the minister had to reply. But what was his reply?
It was that in the case of British Columbia, where the government was turning the money back to the home owners as a partial refund of taxation, it would not be considered taxable for income tax purposes. We welcomed that decision. He also made a pronouncement in respect to the dividend that is being given to the people of Alberta. That, he said, is to be considered income and therefore will be taxable.

subtopic: THEOPHILA YANISHEWSKI LAZORYK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I note that this is the 202nd report of the Senate committee on divorce. I understand we are about half way through the divorce bills which are supposed to come before us this session.
I notice that the Reliable detective agency, previously known as the Fidelity detective agency, has been retained again in connection with this particular case. I also note that in clause 7, lines 2 and 3 have been altered. I think it would be more convenient if hon. members of the house were to have the petition in the form in which it was originally written on the 5th day of December, 1956; that is, printed as written without the amendments being made. The striking out of this section leaves it unclear exactly how this particular paragraph read before the alteration was made.
I am interested in the number of occasions when, apparently, it is necessary to make important changes in sworn statements that were originally presented. In this particular case there is a boy six years of age involved, and according to the evidence given the husband is an alcoholic. She said in her evidence, when asked about her husband:
My husband is an alcoholic and he continuously drinks, and he ran around and never came home. When I asked him when he did come home under the influence of liquor I would ask him where had he been and he would get into a fury and get angry with me and beat me and tell me to mind my own business, and he would go out and not come back for another three or four days.

It is obvious that the hon. members of the other chamber or, indeed, the hon. members of this chamber, have not the facilities at their disposal to deal adequately with an alcoholic who, it is alleged here, was guilty of beating his wife. The wife did take her problems to the appropriate court in Montreal, and did obtain a judgment and a separation as to bed and board. Further, she was given an allowance of $15. The record does not say whether it was $15 a day or $15 a week or $15 a month or $15 a year. Apparently it was not paid very often. I am a little surprised that the evidence did not bring out how frequently this sum of $15 was supposed to have been paid.
I also noticed in the written evidence that the husband apparently is living permanently with some other person. That being the case, I do not see why it was necessary to retain the services of the Reliable dectective agency. It occurs to me that in a very large percentage of the cases which are reaching us this year, when the husband and wife decide they cannot get along together they both appear before the other chamber and seem to tell the whole truth and nothing but the truth; and so long as they indicate that there has not been any collusion the divorce is granted. It would appear to me that this poor woman who is getting $15 periodically from her husband and who also gets $5 a month family allowance-that, of course, will be increased to $6-should not have to be put to the expense of engaging the services of this very costly agency, the Reliable detective agency.
I find that two detectives here gave conflicting evidence. The two detectives concerned were the owner of the agency, Mr. Etheridge, and one of his investigators, Mr. Paquette. Mr. Etheridge in giving his evidence swore that he found the corespondent, whose name is not given, lying in bed. And the other detective, Paquette, swore that the corespondent was sitting; in one place it says "sitting in the bed" and in another it says "sitting on the bed". In any event there is certainly a contradiction in the evidence which these two detectives have given.
In view of these facts I move, seconded by the hon. member for Moose Mountain:
That Bill No. 235 be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills.
It appears to me that these two detectives who were up some time ago on a charge of fabricating evidence should appear before an appropriate committee of this house so we could find out whether or not their evidence appears to have been fabricated.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, March 11, consideration in committee of Bill No. 15, respecting Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company-Mr. Fairey-Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.
On clause 1 - Subdivision of shares.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think when we come to the principle of this bill, contained largely in clause 1, it is well if we examine for a few moments, sir, what are the purposes and duties of parliament. I submit to you, sir, that they are in the main to legislate for the benefit of all the people of Canada, not to become an instrument for the benefit of those who operate on the stock markets, and not to be used in the interests of any special group in the community but in the general interests of the whole Canadian population.
I think you will agree, sir, that there has been a tendency in recent years to use parliament and the legislatures as part of the method by which certain individuals in our society hope to profit from their operation within the particular economy. It is, of course, necessary sometimes to legislate for certain groups on the basis that their activities will redound to the benefit of the whole community; and it is on that basis that parliament and the legislatures on occasion have passed legislation setting up privately-owned corporations to perform certain functions in our economy. Sometimes, sir, we have to legislate in order to enable groups of Canadian citizens to organize themselves into companies and raise funds for carrying out a project which, in the view of parliament, will ultimately redound to the benefit of the whole community.
While I myself am not prone to subscribe to that point of view, I am prepared to admit that in the circumstances of our private enterprise economy it is occasionally necessary to do that in parliament and in the legislatures; but in the case of this particular bill which is before us now, no such consideration arises. We have the evidence of company officials themselves that the company is in no need whatever of raising funds by the sale of its shares, that it has all it requires. We have evidence from the officers that the company's financial situation is unusually healthy,

shall we say; healthy from their point of view but I submit, sir, profoundly unhealthy from the point of view of the unfortunate users of oil in my province of British Columbia.
I should like to place before the committee again the financial position of this company, to show how unnecessary it is for this parliament to act on behalf of the Canadian people and grant any more privileges to this particular group. Their profits in 1955 amounted to $3 million. In 1956 they amounted to over $7 million, and it was estimated for us before the committee-perhaps rather rashly and indiscreetly-by the company's treasurer that if all goes well, this year their profits will amount to over $10 million.
Every now and again during our discussions in the railways, canals and telegraphs committee reference was made to the fact that the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company has not been declared a common carrier. In fact I think it is not too much to say that the company's officers exhibited a certain amount of satisfaction over the fact that their company had not been declared a common carrier; and I can well understand that, sir, when I consult the Pipe Lines Act and find there the provisions governing the actions of a company which has been designated a common carrier by the board of transport commissioners.
In section 39 of the Pipe Lines Act I read this:
The board-
That is the board of transport commissioners.
-may, by order, declare a company to be a common carrier whether the company has or has not acted or held itself out as a common carrier, and the expression "common carrier" in the following sections of this part means a company that has been declared by the board to be a common carrier.
Let us now see what happens to a company which has been so declared a common carrier, presumably in the interests of the Canadian people. I find in section 40 of the Pipe Lines Act the following:
The board may make orders and regulations with respect to all matters relating to traffic, tolls or tariffs.
Section 43 of the act spells out in more detail the obligations a common carrier will be obliged to uphold when it has been declared such. I am sure this section will be of great interest to the oil users on the lower mainland of British Columbia who have been writing to members of parliament in recent weeks protesting the increased oil prices they have been obliged to pay in the last few weeks. Section 43 reads as follows:
All tolls shall be just and reasonable, and shall always, under substantially similar circumstances

and conditions with respect to all traffic of the same description carried over the same route, be charged equally to all persons at the same rate.
I think the oil consumers of British Columbia will be particularly interested in the phrase "just and reasonable" in that section, and they will wonder whether it can be possible for the rates charged by the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company to really be considered just and reasonable when oil prices have been increased since the development of this pipe line-this modern, efficient method of transportation-over the older and more expensive method of bringing oil into the port of Vancouver by tanker.
I believe section 41 of the Pipe Lines Act will also be of interest to the oil consumers of my province. It reads as follows:
(1) Subject to such exceptions, conditions or regulations as the board may prescribe or approve, a common carrier shall, according to its powers, without delay and with due care and diligence, receive, transport and deliver all oil offered for transportation by means of its company pipe line.
That section has great significance in this instance, because we have it on the evidence of the company's officers that a large part of the shares of this company are held by oil companies in the province of Alberta. In fact it is not too much to say that certain oil companies in the province of Alberta control this company, and that therefore it would be very doubtful if other oil companies wishing to get their oil onto the markets of the lower mainland would be given free access to the facilities of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company, as they would if that company were declared to be a common carrier under the Pipe Lines Act.
I submit to you, sir, that it is fear of such a development that causes this company to come before parliament now to seek power to divide its shares by five. It is not, on the basis of the evidence the company offers us, any need or desire to raise more funds from the public by means of the sale of shares, because if that were the case they would have put on the market some of the three and a half million shares still held in the company's treasury. It can only be fear of the public reaction when the mounting profits are expressed, as they will have to be, in terms of so many dollars per outstanding share. When the company has outstanding only some million and a half shares, then the profits they are making at the present time will represent to the public something very much greater than just and reasonable rates could provide.
Private Bills
If, however, in its wisdom parliament were to permit this company to divide its shares by five, then they would be in a position to present to the public a picture of a very modest net return per issued share, a return of about $1.35 in the year 1957 as opposed to $6.60 if the shares are not divided. I suggest to you, sir, that this is the reason the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company is coming before us at the present time to ask for authority to divide its shares in this manner.
I also submit to you, sir, that it is not a part of the duties of parliament to legislate in such a way as to enable any group in the community to deceive the general public as to the real volume of net earnings they are making from a public service such as this the transportation of an essential fuel to the Pacific coast of Canada. For that reason hon. members of this group have protested the passage of this bill ever since it was first brought before the house.
I have not heard the sponsor of this bill present any argument to refute the suggestion I have just made, that it is not any honest or sincere need for further investment of funds in this company that causes them to take this action. It is purely a desire to deceive the public as to the real nature of their net earnings.
May I call it six o'clock, sir?
Progress reported.
